# Factors Affecting Hypertension Treatment Adherence in Older Adults: An Evidence-Based Literature Review

**Prepared:** May 2025  
**Document type:** Evidence-based literature review  
**Approximate manuscript length:** 4,500 words, excluding references  

> **Scope and source note.** This manuscript is written for transfer into a 10–15-page Word document using standard academic formatting (12-point font, double spacing, and 1-inch margins). Because live database access was unavailable during preparation, the review synthesizes peer-reviewed studies and authoritative reports publicly available through the literature known through May 2025. Bibliographic details and local database holdings should be verified before formal submission.

## Factors Affecting Adherence in Hypertension Management

Hypertension is among the most prevalent, consequential, and modifiable cardiovascular risk factors in older adults. In the United States, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) estimates that nearly half of adults have hypertension when hypertension is defined as systolic blood pressure of at least 130 mm Hg, diastolic blood pressure of at least 80 mm Hg, or current antihypertensive medication use. Only approximately one in four adults with hypertension has the condition controlled, although national estimates vary according to the definition, survey period, and measurement method used (CDC, 2024). The American Heart Association (AHA) similarly identifies high blood pressure as a major contributor to coronary heart disease, stroke, heart failure, chronic kidney disease, cognitive decline, disability, and premature death (Martin et al., 2025; Tsao et al., 2023). Prevalence increases sharply with age, making adherence to treatment particularly important in primary care, geriatrics, cardiology, and community health.

Age-stratified national data demonstrate that hypertension is not distributed evenly across adulthood. Using the 2017 American College of Cardiology/AHA threshold of 130/80 mm Hg, National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey estimates have generally found prevalence below 25% among adults aged 18–39 years, approximately 50% among adults aged 40–59 years, and approximately three-quarters among adults aged 60 years or older (Ostchega et al., 2020). Among the “oldest old,” isolated systolic hypertension is especially common because arterial stiffening, endothelial dysfunction, and reduced vascular compliance progressively raise systolic pressure. Nevertheless, age comparisons depend on the operational definition. Studies using the older 140/90 mm Hg threshold report lower absolute prevalence, and studies that classify treated patients as hypertensive produce different estimates from studies using measured pressure alone. These definitional differences must be considered when interpreting trends.

Medication adherence refers to the extent to which a person’s medication-taking behavior corresponds with an agreed treatment plan. It is distinct from persistence, which is the duration of continued therapy, and from therapeutic inertia, which occurs when treatment is not intensified despite uncontrolled blood pressure. Adherence is often operationalized through self-report, pill counts, prescription refill records, the medication possession ratio, proportion of days covered (PDC), electronic monitoring, or biochemical detection of medicines or metabolites. A PDC of at least 80% is widely used to indicate adherence, but it is an imperfect threshold. Refill data show whether medication was available, not whether it was ingested; self-report is vulnerable to recall and social-desirability bias; and biochemical testing can misclassify intermittently adherent patients because of “white-coat adherence” immediately before an appointment (Burnier & Egan, 2019; Vrijens et al., 2012).

Older age does not have a simple, linear relationship with adherence. Adults in the early older-age range, commonly 65–74 years, may adhere better than younger adults because they perceive greater cardiovascular risk, maintain stable routines, and have Medicare or other prescription coverage. With advancing age, however, multimorbidity, frailty, polypharmacy, cognitive and sensory impairment, dysphagia, impaired dexterity, dependence on caregivers, and frequent transitions of care can reverse this advantage. Consequently, adults aged 75–84 years and those aged 85 years or older may be highly adherent when routines and caregiver support are strong, yet particularly vulnerable to unintentional nonadherence when cognitive or functional reserves decline. Many studies collapse everyone aged 65 years or older into one category, obscuring clinically important differences between a healthy 66-year-old and a frail 90-year-old. This is a major limitation in the evidence base.

The World Health Organization’s multidimensional adherence model remains useful for organizing the determinants of hypertension treatment behavior. It identifies socioeconomic, health-system, condition-related, therapy-related, and patient-related influences (World Health Organization, 2003). In older adults, these domains frequently interact. A patient may understand the prescription and intend to follow it but still miss doses because a high copayment delays refills, arthritis prevents opening a bottle, nocturia makes a diuretic unacceptable, or mild cognitive impairment disrupts the dosing sequence. Labeling such behavior as “noncompliance” inaccurately implies willful disobedience and may damage the therapeutic relationship. Contemporary practice instead treats nonadherence as a dynamic behavior that must be assessed without judgment.

Socioeconomic barriers include medication cost, transportation difficulties, unstable housing, low health literacy, food insecurity, and limited access to pharmacies or clinicians. Fixed incomes make even modest copayments consequential for older adults taking multiple medications. Patients may ration tablets, skip medications perceived as less urgent, or prioritize food and housing costs. Insurance reduces but does not eliminate this burden because deductibles, formularies, coverage gaps, prior authorization, and pharmacy network restrictions can interrupt therapy. Racial and ethnic inequities arise from structural barriers, unequal access to continuity of care, differences in neighborhood resources, and prior experiences of discrimination—not from race itself. Black adults in the United States have a disproportionately high burden of hypertension, earlier onset, and more hypertension-attributable complications, while Hispanic, rural, immigrant, and low-income populations may encounter additional language, transportation, and access barriers (CDC, 2024; Martin et al., 2025).

Health-system fragmentation also undermines adherence. Older adults may receive prescriptions from several clinicians, resulting in duplicate therapy, conflicting instructions, or medication lists that no longer reflect actual use. Inadequate visit time can prevent reconciliation and shared decision-making. Medication changes during hospitalization, rehabilitation, and return home create additional discrepancies. Conversely, continuous relationships, accessible follow-up, medication synchronization, home blood-pressure support, and team-based management make adherence easier. The health system should therefore be considered part of the causal pathway rather than treating medication taking as solely the patient’s responsibility.

Therapy-related factors are especially prominent in hypertension because the disease is usually asymptomatic while treatment may produce immediate adverse effects. Dizziness, fatigue, orthostasis, urinary frequency, edema, cough, sexual dysfunction, and perceived cognitive effects can outweigh an abstract future benefit in the patient’s decision. Complex dosing, frequent changes, large tablets, difficult packaging, and multiple daily administrations further increase burden. The risk is amplified by polypharmacy, which is common in older adults with diabetes, dyslipidemia, atrial fibrillation, arthritis, chronic kidney disease, or heart failure. Evidence supports reducing regimen complexity, including once-daily administration and fixed-dose combination therapy when clinically appropriate. A meta-analysis found that fixed-dose combinations were associated with improved antihypertensive adherence and persistence compared with separate pills (Du et al., 2018).

Patient-level determinants include knowledge, beliefs, self-efficacy, perceived necessity, concerns about harm, memory, mood, and daily routines. Self-efficacy—the confidence that one can carry out medication and self-management behaviors despite barriers—is a central, modifiable factor. Patients with greater self-efficacy are more likely to refill prescriptions, use organizational tools, monitor blood pressure, problem-solve after a missed dose, and communicate adverse effects. Education is necessary but not sufficient: a patient may know that hypertension increases stroke risk yet remain unable to afford, tolerate, remember, or physically manage treatment. Education is most effective when paired with skills training, teach-back, simplified instructions, and collaborative goal setting.

Depression, anxiety, social isolation, and low perceived control are associated with poorer self-care. Cognitive impairment can affect prospective memory and executive function before obvious dementia is recognized. Visual impairment may prevent reading labels; hearing impairment may impede verbal counseling; and tremor, neuropathy, or arthritis may prevent the manipulation of packaging. Caregivers can be protective by organizing and administering medications, but caregiver burden or unclear responsibility may also cause omissions. Clinicians should therefore assess who actually fills the pill organizer, requests refills, and observes administration rather than assuming that independent living implies independent medication management.

Poor adherence has substantial morbidity and mortality implications. Antihypertensive treatment reduces major cardiovascular events, and evidence from adults aged 75 years or older demonstrates that appropriately selected older patients benefit from blood-pressure reduction (Williamson et al., 2016). When medicines are not taken consistently, patients remain exposed to stroke, myocardial infarction, heart failure, kidney disease, vascular dementia, hospitalization, disability, and death. In a meta-analysis of cardiovascular preventive treatments, good adherence was associated with an approximately 20% lower risk of cardiovascular disease and a substantially lower risk of all-cause mortality compared with poor adherence, although some of this relationship may reflect healthy-adherer effects (Chowdhury et al., 2013). Cohort evidence has also linked nonadherence to increased stroke and stroke-related death among patients with hypertension (Herttua et al., 2013).

At the population level, high blood pressure is a leading contributor to cardiovascular deaths in the United States. It was a primary or contributing cause of more than 685,000 U.S. deaths in 2022, according to CDC reporting, although this count should not be interpreted as deaths caused specifically by medication nonadherence (CDC, 2024). The proportion directly attributable to nonadherence cannot be isolated reliably because uncontrolled blood pressure may also result from undertreatment, resistant hypertension, measurement error, clinical inertia, access barriers, or intolerance. Nonetheless, observational and intervention evidence consistently supports a pathway from poorer medication implementation to poorer blood-pressure control and, in turn, to cardiovascular and renal harm.

Hypertension also imposes a major financial burden. CDC estimates place U.S. hypertension-related costs at approximately $131–$198 billion annually when health services, medications, and lost productivity are included, based on earlier national cost periods and dollars (CDC, 2024). Published economic estimates vary because some count only direct hypertension treatment while others include attributable cardiovascular and productivity costs. Kirkland et al. (2018) projected that adults with hypertension incur roughly $2,000 more in annual health-care expenditure than those without hypertension, amounting to approximately $131 billion in higher national spending during the study period. Poor adherence can reduce pharmacy spending in the short term but increase emergency visits, hospitalizations, stroke rehabilitation, skilled nursing use, caregiver burden, and long-term disability. Conversely, improved adherence can increase medication expenditures while reducing avoidable medical utilization. Economic evaluation must therefore consider total cost of care rather than pharmacy spending alone.

The evidence establishes adherence as both a clinical and system-level safety issue. Effective management requires identifying each patient’s barriers, matching interventions to those barriers, and avoiding indiscriminate reminders for problems that reminders cannot solve. The remainder of this review evaluates the literature concerning multidisciplinary, psychosocial, patient-centered, and technological strategies relevant to older adults.

## Search Strategy

A structured review strategy was developed using concepts specified for this clinical question: adherence, self-efficacy, hypertension or high blood pressure, older adults, and medication adherence. The intended databases and sources were PubMed/MEDLINE, CINAHL, Google Scholar, CDC, AHA, and reference lists of eligible studies and major systematic reviews. The review focused on literature available in English through May 2025. Priority was given to studies published from January 2015 through May 2025 to represent current treatment and technology; seminal adherence frameworks, landmark trials, and earlier systematic reviews were retained when necessary to explain measurement, determinants, or intervention effectiveness.

A representative PubMed search was: **(“Hypertension”[MeSH] OR hypertension OR “high blood pressure”) AND (“Medication Adherence”[MeSH] OR adheren* OR complian* OR persistence OR “proportion of days covered”) AND (“Aged”[MeSH] OR “Aged, 80 and over”[MeSH] OR “older adult*” OR elder* OR geriatric*) AND (“Self Efficacy”[MeSH] OR self-efficacy OR barrier* OR determinant* OR intervention*)**. Additional combinations included *polypharmacy, health literacy, cost, pharmacist, nurse, multidisciplinary, motivational interviewing, shared decision-making, fixed-dose combination, telehealth, text messaging, mobile health, electronic pillbox,* and *home blood pressure monitoring*. CINAHL searches used comparable subject headings and keywords. Google Scholar was used conceptually for citation chaining and locating open-access versions of relevant articles. CDC and AHA reports were used for current prevalence, mortality, disparities, and cost context rather than treatment-effect estimates.

Studies were eligible when they involved adults with diagnosed hypertension or antihypertensive prescriptions; included older adults, provided an older subgroup, or addressed an intervention directly applicable to older populations; measured medication adherence, persistence, self-efficacy, blood-pressure control, or a closely related implementation outcome; and used a peer-reviewed quantitative, qualitative, mixed-methods, systematic-review, or meta-analytic design. Public reports from recognized government and professional organizations were eligible for epidemiologic context. Intervention studies were included when they evaluated multidisciplinary, psychosocial, patient-centered, regimen-based, or technological approaches.

Studies were excluded when they addressed only pregnancy-related or pediatric hypertension; focused solely on clinician adherence to guidelines; did not distinguish antihypertensive treatment from unrelated medication classes; were editorials without empirical data; or reported no adherence, implementation, persistence, self-efficacy, or blood-pressure outcome. Studies focused exclusively on younger adults were not used as primary evidence for older patients, although broader adult systematic reviews were retained when geriatric-specific intervention literature was limited.

The synthesis was narrative because the literature was heterogeneous in populations, age thresholds, adherence definitions, intervention intensity, follow-up, and outcomes. Evidence was weighted according to design quality, with systematic reviews, meta-analyses, randomized trials, national surveillance, and large cohorts given greater interpretive weight than small single-site studies. Particular attention was paid to whether adherence was measured objectively, whether interventions were multicomponent, whether follow-up was sufficient, and whether older adults with frailty, cognitive impairment, or social disadvantage were represented.

This approach is a structured literature review rather than a fully reproducible systematic review. A live database search, independent dual screening, formal risk-of-bias assessment, and PRISMA flow count were not available in the preparation environment. Therefore, no precise number of screened citations is claimed, and the review avoids presenting an artificial study-selection count. This transparency is important because database indexing and publication status can change through May 2025.

## Results

Across the evidence, no single intervention consistently resolves hypertension nonadherence in older adults. The strongest approaches are multilevel, combining regimen simplification and affordable access with repeated assessment, trusted professional support, self-management skills, and carefully selected technology. Effects on adherence are often modest and may diminish after active support ends. Blood-pressure improvement is more consistently demonstrated than improvement in any single adherence metric, partly because adherence measures capture different stages of medication use.

### Multidisciplinary

Team-based care is one of the most consistently supported strategies for hypertension control. Pharmacists, nurses, nurse practitioners, primary care clinicians, community health workers, social workers, and caregivers address different components of adherence. Pharmacists can reconcile medications, identify therapeutic duplication, synchronize refills, recommend once-daily or fixed-dose combinations, counsel about adverse effects, and communicate recommendations to prescribers. Nurses and nurse practitioners can assess self-efficacy, use teach-back, review home readings, screen for orthostasis or cognitive decline, and provide longitudinal follow-up. Social workers and community health workers can address transportation, benefits, food insecurity, language, and community trust.

The Community Preventive Services Task Force concluded that team-based care improves blood-pressure control and is economically reasonable across diverse settings (Community Preventive Services Task Force, 2021). Proia et al. (2014) found that team-based approaches improved hypertension outcomes when responsibilities were added to or shared among team members. Mills et al. (2018) likewise found that multilevel implementation strategies—including team-based care and health coaching—improved blood-pressure control. Because these programs commonly combine medication management, follow-up, education, and self-monitoring, their effects cannot always be assigned to adherence alone. That is a limitation scientifically but a strength clinically, where the goal is improved outcomes rather than isolation of a single behavioral mechanism.

Pharmacist-led interventions are particularly relevant for polypharmacy. Santschi et al. (2014) reported that pharmacist interventions improved blood pressure in randomized trials, often through counseling, medication review, and collaboration with physicians. In older adults, pharmacists can identify whether apparent nonadherence is an adaptive response to adverse effects or an overly complex regimen. Brown-bag medication review should include prescription medicines, over-the-counter drugs, supplements, and the patient’s real administration schedule. Asking, “How do you take this at home?” is more informative than reciting the electronic list.

Regimen simplification is an essential multidisciplinary intervention because it removes rather than merely compensates for a barrier. Fixed-dose combinations reduce pill burden and may improve persistence and adherence (Du et al., 2018). Synchronizing refill dates, prescribing 90-day supplies, using mail delivery when reliable, and changing from multiple daily doses to once-daily dosing can further reduce implementation failure. These changes must be balanced against the need for cautious titration, renal monitoring, orthostatic symptoms, and the individualized goals recommended for older adults with limited life expectancy or frailty.

Care transitions represent an important multidisciplinary vulnerability. Discharge lists frequently differ from preadmission regimens, and older patients may retain discontinued bottles. A high-value transition process includes medication reconciliation, a clearly marked stop/start/change list, caregiver inclusion, prompt post-discharge contact, and communication with the community pharmacy and primary care team. The adherence plan should name who will obtain, organize, administer, and monitor each medication.

Team care can fail when roles are poorly defined or recommendations are not integrated into prescribing. It also requires reimbursement, interoperable communication, and staffing. Rural and under-resourced clinics may lack embedded pharmacists or care managers. Scalable alternatives include collaborative practice agreements, centralized telepharmacy, nurse-led protocols, and referral pathways to community pharmacists. The central lesson is that older adults should not be expected to coordinate a fragmented system unaided.

### Psychosocial

Psychosocial influences determine whether patients view treatment as necessary, feasible, and congruent with their goals. Hypertension’s asymptomatic nature encourages some patients to take medication only when they “feel pressure,” experience a headache, or obtain a high reading. Others fear dependency, kidney damage, or excessive lowering of blood pressure. These beliefs may be reinforced by prior dizziness, falls, confusing media messages, or experiences within family and community networks. A respectful exploration of concerns is more effective than assuming lack of knowledge.

Self-efficacy provides a useful link between beliefs and action. An older patient with strong self-efficacy can integrate medication into a routine, seek help with side effects, and recover after missed doses. A patient with low self-efficacy may become overwhelmed by a medication change or abnormal home reading. Interventions should build mastery through small, achievable steps: linking medicine to breakfast, practicing pillbox filling, demonstrating home monitoring, using teach-back, and creating a specific plan for missed doses. Progress should be reinforced rather than framed as pass/fail adherence.

Motivational interviewing and shared goal setting can help resolve ambivalence. The clinician may ask what the patient believes the medicine does, what makes it difficult, and which adverse outcome matters most. Stroke prevention, preserving independence, avoiding dialysis, or remaining able to care for a spouse may be more motivating than a numeric pressure target. Conn et al. (2015) found that medication-adherence interventions in hypertensive adults produced small but significant improvements overall, with behavioral components and repeated contact commonly represented among more successful approaches. However, effect sizes varied and many trials did not focus specifically on the oldest adults.

Depression and social isolation warrant direct screening. Depression may reduce concentration, energy, perceived benefit, and problem-solving capacity. Living alone may eliminate cues previously supplied by a spouse, while bereavement can destabilize long-standing routines. Conversely, social support can improve persistence by providing reminders, transportation, emotional encouragement, and assistance communicating with clinicians. Caregiver involvement should occur with patient permission and should not displace autonomy. The patient should remain involved at the highest feasible level.

Cultural humility is essential. Beliefs about hypertension, traditional therapies, diet, and pharmaceuticals vary within as well as between cultural groups. Language-concordant counseling, professional interpretation, plain-language materials, and respect for complementary practices can strengthen trust. Community health workers and faith- or community-based programs may reach patients who distrust or have difficulty accessing traditional systems. Interventions should avoid stereotyping and should examine structural factors, including pharmacy access and historical discrimination.

Financial stress has psychosocial as well as material effects. Patients may feel ashamed to disclose rationing, leading clinicians to increase doses for what appears to be resistant hypertension. A normalizing question—“Many people have trouble affording medicines; has cost caused you to delay or skip any?”—is more likely to elicit an accurate response. Clinicians can then consider generics, lower-cost alternatives, formulary alignment, assistance programs, synchronization, or social-work referral. Cost screening should be repeated because coverage and household circumstances change.

Psychosocial interventions alone are unlikely to correct adverse effects, unaffordable therapy, or severe cognitive impairment. Their value is greatest when paired with structural solutions. The evidence supports a “barrier-to-intervention” match: beliefs call for dialogue; forgetfulness calls for cues and simplification; cost calls for access support; adverse effects call for clinical adjustment; and cognitive impairment calls for caregiver or dispensing assistance.

### Patient-Centered

Patient-centered hypertension management treats the older adult’s goals, function, preferences, health literacy, and treatment burden as core clinical data. It begins by determining whether nonadherence is intentional, unintentional, or mixed. A brief nonjudgmental assessment can ask how many doses were missed in the past week, what happens on weekends or travel days, when the last refill was obtained, and what concerns the patient has. Pharmacy refill data can supplement the discussion. Unexpectedly uncontrolled pressure despite multiple medicines should prompt confirmation of measurement technique, out-of-office readings, adherence assessment, and evaluation for secondary or resistant hypertension before further intensification.

Shared decision-making is especially important because aggressive treatment can produce orthostatic symptoms or conflict with quality-of-life goals in frail adults. The SPRINT trial and its subgroup of adults aged 75 years or older demonstrated cardiovascular and mortality benefits from intensive systolic pressure control among selected ambulatory participants (Williamson et al., 2016; Wright et al., 2015). These findings do not mean that every frail, institutionalized, cognitively impaired, or multimorbid older adult should receive the same target. SPRINT excluded several high-risk groups, including people with diabetes or prior stroke, and trial monitoring was more intensive than routine practice. Individualized targets and close assessment of falls, renal function, electrolytes, and symptoms remain necessary.

Health literacy–responsive communication improves safety and feasibility. Instructions should use plain language, large print, one consistent medication name, and an updated list showing indication and timing. Teach-back should verify the plan without testing the patient: “I want to be sure I explained this clearly. How will you take these pills tomorrow?” Color coding and pictograms may assist some patients, but color should not be the sole identifier because pills and manufacturers change and visual impairment is common.

Patient-centered plans also integrate medication with lifestyle management without implying that lifestyle can always replace necessary treatment. Sodium reduction, physical activity, weight management, moderation of alcohol, tobacco cessation, and a Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension–style eating pattern are evidence-based. Yet recommendations must account for dental problems, mobility, food access, renal disease, cultural diet, and caregiver support. Overly ambitious plans can erode self-efficacy. One or two feasible goals, reviewed at follow-up, are preferable.

Home blood-pressure monitoring can enhance engagement when paired with co-interventions. Tucker et al. (2017) found that self-monitoring was more effective when combined with professional support, medication titration, education, or lifestyle counseling than when used alone. For older adults, clinicians should validate the device, ensure an appropriate cuff, demonstrate seated technique, assess the ability to read and record results, and specify when to contact the clinic. Excessive checking can increase anxiety, while self-adjusting doses in response to a single reading can be dangerous. A written protocol is therefore essential.

Cognitive and functional screening should be integrated into adherence assessment. When decline is identified, possible accommodations include blister packaging, automated dispensing, home nursing, pharmacy delivery, caregiver administration, and simplification. Deprescribing duplicate, nonbeneficial, or burdensome drugs may indirectly improve adherence to essential antihypertensives. The objective is not maximal medication count but the least burdensome regimen that achieves a patient-important benefit.

A practical clinical model is to assess five issues at each uncontrolled-pressure visit: **access, actual use, adverse effects, ability, and attitudes**. Access includes cost and pharmacy availability; actual use includes refill gaps and dosing patterns; adverse effects include orthostasis and urinary symptoms; ability includes cognition, vision, dexterity, and swallowing; attitudes include necessity beliefs and preferences. Documenting the dominant barrier allows the team to choose a proportionate response and evaluate it at a defined interval.

### Technological Intervention

Technology can improve adherence through reminders, monitoring, feedback, and communication, but it is not inherently patient-centered. Available interventions include text messages, smartphone applications, patient portals, automated calls, electronic pillboxes, smart bottle caps, remote blood-pressure monitoring, telehealth, and pharmacy refill alerts. These tools may be particularly helpful for older adults who have stable routines, sufficient sensory and cognitive capacity, reliable connectivity, and willingness to use them.

Text-message interventions show modest benefit across chronic disease and hypertension populations. A randomized trial by Bobrow et al. (2016) found that automated text messages produced a small improvement in blood pressure among adults with hypertension. Thakkar et al. (2016) similarly concluded that mobile text messaging approximately doubled the odds of medication adherence across chronic diseases, although included studies varied and were not limited to older adults or hypertension. The practical effect depends on message frequency, personalization, interactivity, and whether the system connects patients with clinicians who can act on reported problems.

Remote blood-pressure monitoring is more effective when measurements trigger timely clinical action. Simply transmitting readings may generate data without improving care. Successful programs define thresholds, assign responsibility for reviewing alerts, enable medication adjustment, and provide coaching. Older adults may benefit from devices that automatically transmit readings and avoid manual entry. However, false alerts, cuff errors, internet outages, and lack of integration with the electronic health record can create burden.

Electronic pillboxes and smart packaging can provide reminders and implementation data. They may identify whether a compartment was opened, but opening does not prove ingestion. Devices can also be expensive, difficult to fill, incompatible with as-needed medicines, or confusing after regimen changes. Audible alarms may not help patients with hearing impairment; smartphone alerts may not help patients who do not carry or charge a phone. The technology must be tested with the individual rather than prescribed based on age stereotypes.

Digital inequities are a major concern. Adults of advanced age, lower income, limited English proficiency, rural residence, or impaired cognition may have less access to broadband, smartphones, digital literacy training, and technical support. Caregiver-mediated technology can bridge some gaps, but it raises consent, privacy, and workload concerns. Technology should augment—not replace—human contact, affordable medication, and clear instructions. Every digital program should offer a nondigital alternative.

Privacy and data governance also require attention. Remote systems may collect medication behavior, vital signs, and location-linked information. Clinics should explain what is collected, who reviews it, and what response patients can expect. Patients should not infer continuous monitoring if the system is reviewed only during business hours. Technology that detects probable nonadherence should trigger supportive outreach, not punitive labeling.

Overall, technology has the strongest rationale as one component of a multicomponent intervention. Reminder-only approaches address forgetfulness but not cost, beliefs, side effects, or complexity. Remote monitoring plus pharmacist or nurse management, personalized education, and simplified prescribing is more likely to improve blood pressure than a standalone application. Evidence specific to adults aged 85 years or older, patients with cognitive impairment, and long-term care residents remains limited.

## Strengths and Limitations

A principal strength of this review is its integration of epidemiologic, behavioral, clinical, economic, and implementation evidence. The synthesis does not frame nonadherence as an isolated patient failure; instead, it considers medication burden, access, care fragmentation, cognition, self-efficacy, social context, and intervention design. It also distinguishes adherence from persistence and therapeutic inertia, emphasizes the heterogeneity of older adults, and organizes interventions into domains that can be translated into clinical practice. National surveillance and professional guidance provide current context, while systematic reviews, randomized trials, and cohort studies support conclusions regarding intervention effectiveness and clinical consequences.

The review also emphasizes clinically actionable findings. Regimen simplification, fixed-dose combinations, affordability screening, team-based care, teach-back, caregiver engagement, and supported home monitoring are feasible in many settings. The “access, actual use, adverse effects, ability, and attitudes” assessment can be embedded into hypertension follow-up. The focus on barrier-matched intervention reduces the likelihood of applying ineffective reminders to structural or pharmacologic problems.

Several limitations constrain interpretation. First, the review was prepared without live access to PubMed, CINAHL, or Google Scholar. It is therefore a structured narrative synthesis rather than a fully reproducible systematic review, and recent in-press studies or updated surveillance releases through May 2025 may not be represented. Database-specific search exports, deduplication, dual independent screening, PRISMA flow documentation, and formal study-level risk-of-bias scoring were not performed.

Second, adherence research is highly heterogeneous. Self-report tends to overestimate adherence, refill measures do not confirm ingestion, electronic devices alter behavior and measure container opening, and biochemical assays provide only a short observation window. Common 80% thresholds may not represent the same clinical exposure across drug classes or dosing patterns. Differences in hypertension thresholds and blood-pressure measurement further limit comparisons.

Third, causal inference is difficult. Patients who adhere may also exercise more, attend appointments, avoid smoking, and engage in other protective behaviors. This healthy-adherer effect may inflate associations between adherence and mortality. Conversely, sicker or frailer patients may discontinue medication because of adverse effects or end-of-life goals, which can make nonadherence appear more harmful. Randomized adherence interventions avoid some confounding but often have short follow-up and are not powered for cardiovascular events or mortality.

Fourth, older adults are undercharacterized. Many studies use mean age, include relatively healthy volunteers, or define older age as 60 or 65 years without reporting 65–74, 75–84, and 85 years or older separately. Patients with dementia, frailty, multimorbidity, institutional residence, sensory impairment, limited English proficiency, or caregiver dependence are often excluded. Consequently, evidence is least certain for populations at greatest risk of unintentional nonadherence.

Finally, many effective interventions are multicomponent. This makes it difficult to determine whether improvement resulted from counseling, medication intensification, reminders, refill support, or more frequent contact. Blood-pressure control may improve despite unchanged measured adherence, and adherence may improve without sufficient medication intensity. Future studies should measure both implementation behavior and treatment quality.

## Conclusion

Hypertension is highly prevalent in later life and remains a leading preventable contributor to cardiovascular and renal morbidity, disability, mortality, and health-care expenditure. Approximately three-quarters of U.S. adults aged 60 years or older meet contemporary hypertension criteria, although estimates vary by definition and period. Adherence may be relatively strong in younger-old adults but becomes increasingly vulnerable to polypharmacy, cognitive and functional decline, adverse effects, financial strain, and fragmented care as age advances. Existing studies too often conceal this variation by treating all adults aged 65 years or older as one group.

Poor adherence is associated with uncontrolled pressure, stroke, myocardial infarction, heart failure, kidney disease, hospitalization, and death. The exact fraction of hypertension-attributable events caused by nonadherence cannot be determined because clinical inertia, access, resistant hypertension, and measurement error also contribute. Nevertheless, the convergence of observational, trial, and implementation evidence demonstrates that medication implementation and persistence are essential components of effective management.

The evidence favors multicomponent, barrier-matched care. Team-based management, pharmacist and nurse involvement, regimen simplification, fixed-dose combinations, affordability assistance, motivational and self-efficacy support, shared decision-making, caregiver participation, and supported home monitoring are more defensible than education or reminders alone. Technology can extend care but must be simple, equitable, connected to clinical action, and offered alongside nondigital options.

In the clinical setting, adherence should be evaluated routinely and without blame. For every patient with uncontrolled blood pressure, clinicians should assess access, actual medication use, adverse effects, ability to self-manage, and attitudes toward treatment before intensifying therapy. The plan should reflect the patient’s cardiovascular risk, function, goals, life expectancy, and treatment burden. Such an approach supports safer prescribing, better education, stronger therapeutic relationships, and more effective hypertension control.

## Future Research

Future studies should report age in clinically meaningful groups, including 65–74, 75–84, and 85 years or older, and should examine effect modification by frailty, cognitive status, multimorbidity, race and ethnicity, rurality, income, language, and caregiver availability. Long-term care residents, homebound adults, and patients with dementia should be included rather than routinely excluded. Researchers should also distinguish intentional nonadherence, unintentional nonadherence, initiation failure, poor implementation, and discontinuation.

Measurement needs standardization. Trials should combine refill measures or electronic monitoring with validated self-report and, when justified, biochemical methods. Blood-pressure technique and out-of-office confirmation should be specified. Studies should report adherence as a continuous measure as well as a threshold and should assess persistence beyond 12 months. Core outcomes should include blood-pressure control, orthostatic symptoms, falls, quality of life, treatment burden, emergency care, hospitalization, cardiovascular events, mortality, and caregiver outcomes.

Comparative-effectiveness studies are needed to determine which intervention works for which barrier. Examples include pharmacist management versus nurse-led coaching; fixed-dose combinations versus reminder technology; caregiver-supported dispensing versus automated packaging; and remote monitoring with versus without medication titration. Adaptive designs could begin with low-intensity support and escalate according to refill gaps, pressure response, or patient preference.

Digital research should prioritize accessibility and equity. Investigators should evaluate voice-based tools, passive transmission, multilingual systems, large-print interfaces, technical support, and caregiver-linked platforms. Studies must assess privacy, alert fatigue, workflow integration, and the possibility that technology widens disparities. Nondigital comparators should be maintained.

Economic studies should use a health-system and societal perspective, accounting for medication cost, personnel time, technology, transportation, caregiver labor, hospitalization, rehabilitation, long-term care, and productivity. Cost-effectiveness should be reported separately for robust, frail, rural, and socially disadvantaged older adults. Research should also evaluate policy interventions such as copayment elimination, 90-day dispensing, pharmacy synchronization, home delivery, and reimbursement for team-based adherence management.

For practice improvement, clinics should develop an adherence dashboard that combines repeat blood pressure, refill history, medication reconciliation, documented barriers, and follow-up completion. A pragmatic quality-improvement cycle could identify older patients with uncontrolled pressure or PDC below 80%, perform the five-domain assessment, assign a matched intervention, and reassess in four to twelve weeks. Outcomes should be stratified by age, race and ethnicity, language, insurance, and geography to ensure that improvement does not conceal widening inequity.

- **Other systems:** No additional concerns reported.

## O — Objective

### Vital Signs
- Temperature: 102°F
- Pulse: 98 beats/min
- Respiratory rate: 20 breaths/min
- Blood pressure: 122/65 mmHg
- Oxygen saturation: 93% on room air
- Height: 67 in
- Weight: 145 lb
- BMI: 23 kg/m²

### Physical Examination
- **General:** Pleasant, alert, and in no acute distress.
- **Skin:** Warm; no discoloration or cyanosis.
- **Head:** Normocephalic.
- **Eyes:** PERRLA; EOMI.
- **Ears:** Tympanic membranes intact bilaterally without erythema.
- **Nose/Sinuses:** No sinus tenderness.
- **Mouth/Throat:** Pharynx clear; no tonsillar enlargement or exudate.
- **Neck:** Trachea midline; no tenderness or lymphadenopathy.
- **Respiratory:** Bronchial breath sounds and inspiratory crackles over the right lower lobe. Respiratory rate 20/min. No cyanosis.
- **Cardiovascular:** Regular rate and rhythm; normal S1 and S2; no murmurs.
- **Abdomen:** Soft, round, and non-tender; active bowel sounds.
- **Musculoskeletal:** Strength 5/5 and full range of motion in all extremities.
- **Neurologic:** Alert and oriented ×4; coherent thought processes; no gross focal deficits.
- **Lymphatic:** No lymphadenopathy appreciated.

### Diagnostic Studies
- **Chest radiograph, two views:** Right lower lobe consolidation, consistent with pneumonia.

---

## A — Assessment

### 1. Community-Acquired Pneumonia, Right Lower Lobe
**Most likely diagnosis.** Acute high fever, rigors, productive cough, pleuritic right-sided chest pain, focal bronchial breath sounds and inspiratory crackles, and radiographic right lower lobe consolidation are consistent with community-acquired bacterial pneumonia.

- **ICD-10-CM:** J18.9, Pneumonia, unspecified organism
- Possible pathogens include *Streptococcus pneumoniae*, *Haemophilus influenzae*, and atypical organisms.
- Oxygen saturation is mildly reduced at 93% on room air, but the patient is hemodynamically stable, not confused, and not in acute respiratory distress.
- **CRB-65:** 0 based on available findings, supporting outpatient treatment with close monitoring.

### 2. Fever Secondary to Pneumonia
- **ICD-10-CM:** R50.9

### 3. Pleuritic Right-Sided Chest Pain Secondary to Pneumonia
- **ICD-10-CM:** R07.81
- Pain is localized, nonradiating, and associated with coughing, supporting a pleuritic rather than ischemic cause.

### 4. Mild Hypoxemia
- Oxygen saturation 93% on room air, likely secondary to right lower lobe consolidation.

### Differential Diagnoses
- Influenza or COVID-19 with secondary bacterial pneumonia
- Viral lower respiratory tract infection
- Acute bronchitis, less likely given focal examination findings and radiographic consolidation
- Pulmonary embolism, less likely given high fever, purulent sputum, focal crackles, and radiographic consolidation, but should be reconsidered if symptoms evolve or treatment response is inadequate

---

## P — Plan

### Diagnostics
1. Chest radiograph completed and confirms right lower lobe consolidation.
2. Obtain or consider:
   - Rapid COVID-19 and influenza testing due to fever, respiratory symptoms, and occupational exposure
   - CBC with differential
   - Basic or comprehensive metabolic panel
3. Blood cultures are not routinely required for stable outpatient CAP but should be obtained if the patient becomes toxic, hypotensive, requires hospitalization, or fails outpatient therapy.
4. Sputum culture is not routinely necessary for uncomplicated outpatient CAP; consider if symptoms worsen, resistant infection is suspected, or initial treatment fails.
5. Recheck pulse oximetry before discharge and with ambulation if available.

### Pharmacologic Treatment
1. **Doxycycline 100 mg PO twice daily for 5–7 days**, selected because of reported penicillin and sulfonamide allergies.
   - Take with a full glass of water.
   - Remain upright for at least 30 minutes after each dose.
   - Avoid taking at the same time as antacids, iron, calcium, or magnesium supplements.
   - Use sun protection due to photosensitivity risk.
   - Continue treatment until clinically stable and afebrile for at least 48–72 hours; reassess if not improving.

2. **Fever and pleuritic discomfort:**
   - Acetaminophen 650 mg PO every 6 hours as needed; maximum 3,000 mg/day unless otherwise directed.
   - Alternatively, ibuprofen 400 mg PO every 6–8 hours with food as needed if no kidney disease, gastrointestinal bleeding, anticoagulant use, or other contraindication.
   - Avoid exceeding labeled dosing or combining products containing acetaminophen.

3. **Cough management:**
   - Encourage hydration and humidified air.
   - Consider guaifenesin as directed on the OTC label to assist expectoration.
   - Avoid routine cough suppression when the cough is effectively clearing secretions. If sleep remains significantly impaired, a nighttime antitussive may be considered after medication interaction review.

### Supportive Care and Education
- Increase oral fluids and rest.
- Monitor temperature and respiratory symptoms.
- Avoid work, particularly direct patient care, until afebrile for at least 24 hours without antipyretics and otherwise meeting employer/infection-control return-to-work requirements.
- Reinforce hand hygiene, cough etiquette, and masking while symptomatic.
- Discussed that sputum color alone does not identify the causative organism, but the overall findings and CXR support bacterial pneumonia.
- Reviewed medication adherence and potential adverse effects.

### Follow-Up
- Telephone or in-person reassessment within **24–48 hours** due to oxygen saturation of 93% and high fever.
- Return visit in **48–72 hours** if there is no clear clinical improvement.
- Consider repeat chest radiograph in approximately **6 weeks** if symptoms persist, clinical recovery is incomplete, or another indication develops. Routine repeat imaging may not be necessary if she has complete clinical resolution and remains low risk.

### Emergency Precautions
The patient should seek emergency care immediately for:
- Increasing shortness of breath or respiratory distress
- Oxygen saturation persistently **≤92%** on room air, if home monitoring is available
- Cyanosis
- Confusion, syncope, or marked lethargy
- Persistent or worsening chest pain, especially pain unrelated to coughing or pain with radiation
- Hemoptysis
- Inability to maintain hydration or take oral medication
- Persistent high fever or rapidly worsening symptoms
- Hypotension or other signs of sepsis

**Disposition:** Outpatient treatment is reasonable at present because the patient is alert, hemodynamically stable, and without acute respiratory distress. Close follow-up is required because of mild hypoxemia and high fever.

## Slide 3 — Learning Objectives

By the end of this presentation, learners will be able to:

## Slide 4 — What Is Hypertension?

- **Blood pressure (BP)** is the force exerted by circulating blood against arterial walls.
- **Systolic blood pressure (SBP):** pressure during ventricular contraction.
- **Diastolic blood pressure (DBP):** pressure during ventricular relaxation.
- Hypertension is **persistently elevated BP**, confirmed through proper measurement and repeated assessment.
- ACC/AHA classifies hypertension as:
  - **Stage 1:** SBP 130–139 **or** DBP 80–89 mm Hg
  - **Stage 2:** SBP ≥140 **or** DBP ≥90 mm Hg
- Diagnosis should not ordinarily be based on one isolated reading.

**Key principle:** If SBP and DBP fall into different categories, use the **higher category**.

**Speaker notes:**  
The diagnostic threshold and the threshold for starting medication are not always identical. Treatment decisions also depend on cardiovascular risk, comorbidities, degree of elevation, and confirmation with repeated or out-of-office readings.

---

## Slide 5 — Adult Blood Pressure Categories

| Category | Systolic BP |  | Diastolic BP |
|---|---:|:---:|---:|
| Normal | <120 mm Hg | **and** | <80 mm Hg |
| Elevated | 120–129 mm Hg | **and** | <80 mm Hg |
| Stage 1 hypertension | 130–139 mm Hg | **or** | 80–89 mm Hg |
| Stage 2 hypertension | ≥140 mm Hg | **or** | ≥90 mm Hg |
| Severe hypertension* | >180 mm Hg | **and/or** | >120 mm Hg |

\*Severe readings require prompt reassessment and evaluation for acute target-organ injury.

**Pre-test answer:** **D. 146/92 mm Hg**

**Speaker notes:**  
These are the adult categories used by the ACC/AHA. The American Heart Association’s public education materials reflect these categories. A reading above 180/120 mm Hg is not automatically a hypertensive emergency; emergency status depends on evidence of acute target-organ injury.

---

## Slide 6 — Pathophysiology

### Core relationship

> **Blood Pressure = Cardiac Output × Systemic Vascular Resistance**

Persistent elevation may result from:

- Increased sympathetic nervous system activity
- Activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system
- Sodium and water retention
- Endothelial dysfunction and reduced vasodilation
- Increased systemic vascular resistance
- Vascular remodeling and arterial stiffness
- Genetic, environmental, metabolic, and renal influences

### Progressive damage

Sustained pressure causes endothelial injury and organ damage involving the:

- Heart
- Brain
- Kidneys
- Retina
- Peripheral arteries and aorta

**Speaker notes:**  
Explain that primary hypertension is usually multifactorial rather than caused by one abnormality. Chronic pressure overload promotes left ventricular hypertrophy, atherosclerosis, nephron loss, and further BP elevation—a self-reinforcing cycle.

---

## Slide 7 — Types and Causes of Hypertension

### Primary hypertension

- Accounts for most adult cases
- Develops gradually
- Results from interacting genetic, age-related, environmental, and lifestyle factors

### Secondary hypertension

May be caused by:

- Chronic kidney disease
- Primary aldosteronism
- Renal artery stenosis
- Obstructive sleep apnea
- Thyroid or parathyroid disease
- Pheochromocytoma or Cushing syndrome
- Aortic coarctation
- Pregnancy-related disorders
- Medications/substances:
  - NSAIDs
  - Decongestants
  - Stimulants
  - Corticosteroids
  - Estrogen-containing contraceptives
  - Calcineurin inhibitors
  - Licorice, cocaine, or amphetamines

**Consider secondary causes when HTN is:** abrupt, severe, resistant, occurs at an unusual age, or is associated with hypokalemia or suggestive symptoms.

---

## Slide 8 — Risk Factors

### Nonmodifiable

- Increasing age
- Family history/genetic predisposition
- Race and social risk patterns
- Personal history of cardiovascular or kidney disease

### Modifiable

- Tobacco/nicotine exposure
- High-sodium, low-potassium dietary pattern
- Overweight or obesity
- Physical inactivity
- Excess alcohol intake
- Poor sleep or obstructive sleep apnea
- Diabetes and dyslipidemia
- Chronic stress
- Inconsistent access to care or medication
- Use of BP-raising medications or substances

### Nursing perspective

Assess social determinants affecting:

- Food choices
- Medication affordability
- Transportation
- Health literacy
- Safe spaces for exercise
- Home BP monitor access

**Speaker notes:**  
Avoid framing hypertension solely as a consequence of individual choices. Structural barriers, medication costs, food access, stress, and health care access strongly affect prevention and control.

---

## Slide 9 — Clinical Manifestations and Complications

### Often asymptomatic

Hypertension is frequently called a **“silent” condition** because patients may feel well despite substantial risk.

### Possible but nonspecific symptoms

- Headache
- Dizziness
- Blurred vision
- Palpitations
- Fatigue
- Epistaxis

These symptoms do **not** reliably confirm or exclude HTN.

### Target-organ complications

- **Heart:** coronary artery disease, myocardial infarction, heart failure, left ventricular hypertrophy
- **Brain:** transient ischemic attack, ischemic or hemorrhagic stroke, cognitive impairment
- **Kidneys:** albuminuria and chronic kidney disease
- **Eyes:** hypertensive retinopathy
- **Vasculature:** peripheral artery disease and aortic disease

**Speaker notes:**  
Reinforce that absence of symptoms does not mean absence of harm. Do not attribute headache or dizziness to hypertension without assessing other potential causes.

---

## Slide 10 — How Blood Pressure Is Measured

```text
                 PATIENT POSITION
          ┌───────────────────────────┐
          │ Back supported            │
          │ Quiet; no talking         │
          │ Feet flat, legs uncrossed │
          └───────────────────────────┘

                    Upper arm
                       │
              ┌────────────────┐
              │   BP CUFF      │  ← Lower edge 2–3 cm
              │   centered     │     above antecubital space
              └────────────────┘
                       │
                       ▼  Brachial artery
                [●] Stethoscope
                       │
          ──────────────────────────
             Arm supported at heart level

   Wrong cuff size → inaccurate result
   Arm below heart → reading may be falsely high
   Unsupported back/feet → reading may be falsely high
```

### Before measuring

- Avoid exercise, caffeine, and nicotine for at least 30 minutes when feasible.
- Empty the bladder.
- Rest quietly for at least 5 minutes.
- Remove clothing covering the cuff site.
- Use a validated, calibrated device.

**Speaker notes:**  
Demonstrate with an actual cuff if possible. Cuff bladder dimensions should be appropriate for arm circumference. A cuff that is too small tends to overestimate BP; one that is too large may underestimate it.

---

## Slide 11 — Accurate Measurement Procedure

1. Seat the patient with back supported, feet flat, and legs uncrossed.
2. Support the bare arm at heart level with palm upward.
3. Choose the correct cuff size for arm circumference.
4. Place the cuff over the brachial artery.
5. At the initial visit, measure BP in **both arms**.
6. Obtain at least **two readings**, approximately 1 minute apart, and average them.
7. Use the arm with the higher reading for subsequent measurements when appropriate.
8. Record:
   - BP and arm used
   - Position
   - Cuff size
   - Relevant symptoms or recent exposures
9. Consider standing BP when orthostatic hypotension is suspected.

### Manual auscultation

- First Korotkoff sound = **SBP**
- Disappearance of sounds = **DBP**

**Interactive prompt:** Identify three common errors that could falsely elevate a reading.

**Speaker notes:**  
Possible answers include talking, crossed legs, unsupported arm, full bladder, recent smoking/caffeine/exercise, cuff over clothing, wrong cuff size, and failure to rest.

---

## Slide 12 — Confirming the Diagnosis

### Office assessment

- Obtain an average from at least two careful readings on at least two occasions unless the clinical situation requires immediate action.
- Review previous readings and measurement quality.

### Out-of-office confirmation

- **Home blood pressure monitoring (HBPM)**
- **Ambulatory blood pressure monitoring (ABPM):** often considered the reference standard for out-of-office confirmation

These help identify:

- **White-coat hypertension:** high office BP, lower out-of-office BP
- **Masked hypertension:** normal office BP, high out-of-office BP
- Nocturnal hypertension and abnormal nighttime patterns

### History and physical examination

Assess:

- Cardiovascular risk and family history
- Medication/substance use
- Diet, activity, nicotine, alcohol, and sleep
- Adherence and barriers
- Signs of target-organ damage or secondary causes

---

## Slide 13 — Diagnostic Evaluation

### Common baseline tests

- Urinalysis
- Urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio
- Serum electrolytes
- Blood urea nitrogen and creatinine/eGFR
- Fasting glucose or hemoglobin A1C
- Lipid profile
- Complete blood count
- Thyroid-stimulating hormone
- Electrocardiogram

### Additional tests when indicated

- Echocardiogram
- Sleep study
- Renal imaging or renal artery evaluation
- Aldosterone-renin testing
- Plasma or urinary metanephrines
- Other endocrine testing
- Funduscopic examination

### Goals

- Estimate cardiovascular risk
- Detect target-organ damage
- Identify comorbidities
- Screen for secondary causes
- Establish baseline values before therapy

**Speaker notes:**  
Testing should be individualized. Creatinine and electrolytes are particularly important before and after starting medications that alter kidney function or potassium levels.

---

## Slide 14 — Non-Pharmacologic Treatment

| Intervention | Patient-centered approach |
|---|---|
| Healthy dietary pattern | Emphasize vegetables, fruits, whole grains, legumes, nuts, fish, and low-fat dairy |
| Reduce sodium | Aim for <1,500 mg/day when achievable, or reduce usual intake by at least 1,000 mg/day |
| Increase dietary potassium | Encourage potassium-rich foods unless contraindicated by kidney disease or medications |
| Weight management | Set realistic, sustainable goals |
| Physical activity | About 150 minutes/week of moderate aerobic activity plus resistance exercise |
| Limit alcohol | No more than 2 drinks/day for men and 1 drink/day for women; less is better |
| Tobacco cessation | Offer counseling and evidence-based cessation treatment |
| Improve sleep | Screen for sleep apnea and support regular sleep habits |
| Stress management | Breathing exercises, mindfulness, counseling, and social support |
| Self-monitoring | Use a validated upper-arm home device and maintain a BP log |

**Speaker notes:**  
Lifestyle interventions are recommended for all BP categories and continue even when medication is prescribed. Potassium supplementation or high-potassium diets may be unsafe in advanced kidney disease or with potassium-retaining drugs.

---

## Slide 15 — Pharmacologic Treatment

### Common first-line medication classes

| Class | Examples | Key nursing considerations |
|---|---|---|
| Thiazide-type diuretic | Chlorthalidone, hydrochlorothiazide | Monitor sodium, potassium, uric acid, glucose, and volume status |
| ACE inhibitor | Lisinopril, enalapril | Monitor creatinine and potassium; cough/angioedema risk; avoid in pregnancy |
| Angiotensin receptor blocker | Losartan, valsartan | Monitor creatinine and potassium; avoid in pregnancy |
| Calcium channel blocker | Amlodipine, diltiazem* | Edema; constipation; monitor heart rate with non-dihydropyridines |

\*Selection depends on clinical indication.

### Important principles

- Medication choice is individualized by BP level, cardiovascular risk, comorbidities, age, pregnancy potential, cost, and tolerance.
- Stage 2 HTN often requires **two first-line agents from different classes**, particularly when BP is substantially above goal.
- Avoid routine ACE inhibitor plus ARB combination therapy.
- Beta-blockers are generally reserved for compelling indications such as ischemic heart disease, certain arrhythmias, or heart failure.
- Reassess BP, adherence, adverse effects, kidney function, and electrolytes after initiation or titration.

**Speaker notes:**  
Treatment goals should be individualized. For many adults with confirmed hypertension, a goal below 130/80 mm Hg is recommended when tolerated, but clinical judgment and current protocols should guide care.

---

## Slide 16 — Severe Hypertension and Nursing Priorities

### BP >180 and/or >120 mm Hg

1. Keep the patient seated and repeat the measurement using correct technique.
2. Assess for acute target-organ injury.

### Emergency warning signs

- Chest pain
- Severe dyspnea or pulmonary edema
- New neurologic deficit, confusion, or seizure
- Sudden vision change
- Syncope
- Severe back pain suggesting aortic disease
- Findings of acute kidney injury
- Pregnancy with concerning symptoms

### Response

- **Severe BP with acute target-organ injury:** hypertensive emergency → immediate emergency evaluation and controlled IV treatment.
- **Severe BP without acute injury:** prompt clinician evaluation and timely adjustment of oral therapy; avoid rapid, unmonitored BP reduction.

**Speaker notes:**  
A hypertensive emergency is defined by acute organ injury—not by the BP number alone. Follow institutional emergency protocols. Do not advise a patient to double medication unless specifically directed by the prescribing clinician.

---

## Slide 17 — Patient Education and Adherence Strategies

### Use a patient-centered approach

- Ask: **“What concerns you most about your blood pressure?”**
- Use plain language and professional interpreters when needed.
- Explain that HTN may cause no symptoms but can still damage organs.
- Use **teach-back**:
  - “Please show me how you will measure your BP at home.”
- Use motivational interviewing and shared decision-making.
- Link medication dosing to daily routines.
- Simplify regimens and use once-daily or combination therapy when appropriate.
- Discuss adverse effects proactively.
- Address cost, transportation, food access, and pharmacy barriers.
- Provide written goals, a BP log, and clear follow-up instructions.

### Home BP monitoring education

- Use a validated upper-arm device.
- Measure at consistent times after quiet rest.
- Take two readings about 1 minute apart.
- Record readings rather than reacting to one isolated value.
- Bring the monitor and log to appointments.

### Safety education

- Do not stop medication because BP improves.
- Seek urgent help for severe BP accompanied by warning symptoms.
- Keep follow-up and laboratory appointments.

---

## Slide 18 — Case Study and Clinical Application

### Patient

**Mr. J**, age 52:

- Office BP: 148/94 and 146/92 mm Hg after correct rest and positioning
- Smokes 1 pack/day
- BMI: 31 kg/m²
- Sedentary lifestyle
- Eats frequent processed foods
- Father had myocardial infarction at age 54
- No current chest pain, dyspnea, neurologic deficit, or vision change
- Takes ibuprofen frequently for back pain

### Small-group questions

1. How would you classify his BP?
2. Which modifiable and nonmodifiable risk factors are present?
3. What additional history, examination, and tests are needed?
4. What initial interventions should be discussed?
5. What patient education and follow-up are priorities?

### Suggested clinical application

- **Classification:** Stage 2 hypertension
- Confirm with repeated standardized measurements and HBPM/ABPM as appropriate.
- Assess cardiovascular risk, target-organ damage, secondary contributors, and NSAID use.
- Initiate intensive lifestyle intervention:
  - Tobacco cessation support
  - Sodium reduction/DASH-style eating pattern
  - Physical activity and weight management
- Discuss antihypertensive medication; two first-line agents may be appropriate after clinical evaluation.
- Arrange timely follow-up and monitor creatinine and electrolytes.

**Speaker notes:**  
Ask learners to prioritize nursing actions rather than merely name medications. Explore readiness to stop smoking using motivational interviewing: “On a scale of 0–10, how ready are you to make a quit attempt?” His family history is nonmodifiable, but tobacco use, diet, weight, activity, and frequent NSAID exposure can be addressed.

---

## Slide 19 — Key Takeaways

- Hypertension is common, frequently asymptomatic, and clinically important.
- Stage 1 HTN begins at **130–139 or 80–89 mm Hg**.
- Stage 2 HTN begins at **≥140 or ≥90 mm Hg**.
- Accurate technique and repeated or out-of-office measurements are essential.
- Evaluate cardiovascular risk, target-organ damage, comorbidities, and secondary causes.
- Lifestyle treatment is foundational for every patient.
- Medication selection and BP goals must be individualized.
- Severe BP plus acute target-organ injury is an emergency.
- Nurses improve outcomes through measurement accuracy, education, monitoring, advocacy, and follow-up.

### Exit reflection

**Name one change you will make in your next blood pressure assessment or patient-education encounter.**

---

## Slide 20 — References

American College of Cardiology. (2024). *2024 ACC expert consensus decision pathway for treatment of heart failure with reduced ejection fraction*. https://www.acc.org/

American Heart Association. (2024). *Understanding blood pressure readings*. https://www.heart.org/en/health-topics/high-blood-pressure/understanding-blood-pressure-readings

Carey, R. M., Moran, A. E., Whelton, P. K., & Wright, J. T., Jr. (2022). Treatment of hypertension: A review. *JAMA, 328*(18), 1849–1861. https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2022.19590

Muntner, P., Shimbo, D., Carey, R. M., Charleston, J. B., Gaillard, T., Misra, S., Myers, M. G., Ogedegbe, G., Schwartz, J. E., Townsend, R. R., Urbina, E. M., Viera, A. J., White, W. B., & Wright, J. T., Jr. (2019). Measurement of blood pressure in humans: A scientific statement from the American Heart Association. *Hypertension, 73*(5), e35–e66. https://doi.org/10.1161/HYP.0000000000000087

U.S. Preventive Services Task Force. (2021). Screening for hypertension in adults: US Preventive Services Task Force reaffirmation recommendation statement. *JAMA, 325*(16), 1650–1656. https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2021.4987
