# DOUBLE-SIDED BUYER BROCHURE  
## Word-Ready Copy | Sarasota, Florida

> **Production note:** I cannot access the linked PDF or generate an attached `.docx` here. The brochure below is complete, editable content for a **two-page, double-sided Word document**. It is based on the widely circulated **“132 Things REALTORS® Do for Buyers”** checklist and common Florida buyer-representation practices. Confirm item wording against your copy of the PDF and have your broker review the compensation and legal language before publication.

---

# SIDE 1 — FROM CONSULTATION TO OFFER

**Suggested Word layout:** Landscape • Three columns • 0.5-inch margins  
**Visual theme:** Sarasota coastal blue, sea-glass green, white, and warm sand  
**Suggested image:** Sarasota-area gated-community entrance or Florida single-family home with a pool

---

## PANEL 1 — FRONT COVER

### YOUR SARASOTA HOME-BUYING JOURNEY  
## Expert guidance—from our first conversation through closing

Buying your first home is exciting, but it involves more than finding a beautiful property. Your REALTOR® helps you prepare financially, evaluate communities, understand market conditions, structure a competitive offer, manage deadlines, and coordinate the many professionals involved in the transaction.

### Looking for a single-family home in a gated community?

We will focus on the details that matter to you, including:

- Location and commute
- Price range and monthly-payment comfort
- Gated access and security features
- Community amenities
- HOA fees, rules, reserves, and approval requirements
- Flood zones and insurance considerations
- Property condition and future maintenance
- Resale potential

### YOUR ADVOCATE. YOUR STRATEGY. YOUR HOME.

**[Agent Name], REALTOR®**  
**[Brokerage Name]**  
[Phone] • [Email]  
[Website]  
[Office Address]

**[Insert headshot]**  **[Insert QR code to consultation page]**

---

## PANEL 2 — STARTING WITH A BUYER CONSULTATION

### 1. Buyer Consultation

Our first meeting creates the roadmap for your purchase. Your REALTOR® will:

- Discuss your goals, preferred timing, lifestyle, and long-term plans
- Explain the buying process from financing through closing
- Identify preferred Sarasota-area locations and community features
- Distinguish your **must-haves**, preferences, and deal-breakers
- Review your target price range and estimated ownership expenses
- Discuss lender preapproval and financing options
- Explain current market conditions and negotiation considerations
- Review agency relationships and how your REALTOR® represents you
- Explain the Buyer Broker Agreement, services, term, scope, and compensation
- Establish communication preferences and next steps

### Prepare for Our Meeting

Please bring or consider:

- Photo identification
- Preferred monthly-payment range
- Available down payment and closing funds
- Employment and income information for your lender
- Desired move-in date
- Preferred neighborhoods and commute needs
- Amenity priorities
- Questions about HOA living, insurance, or financing

> **First-time buyer tip:** The purchase price is only one part of affordability. Your estimated monthly cost may include principal, interest, property taxes, homeowners insurance, flood insurance, mortgage insurance, HOA assessments, and community fees.

---

## PANEL 3 — BUYER BROKER AGREEMENT

### Why Is a Written Agreement Needed Before Touring?

Under nationwide practice changes implemented in **August 2024** following the National Association of REALTORS® settlement, MLS participants working with buyers must enter into a **written buyer agreement before touring a home**. This applies to in-person and live virtual tours.

The agreement should clearly describe:

- The real estate services your agent will provide
- The length and geographic or property scope of the relationship
- Whether the representation is exclusive or non-exclusive
- The agent’s compensation and how it is determined
- The buyer’s responsibilities
- How the agreement may be modified or terminated
- Any other brokerage-specific terms

### What It Does *Not* Mean

- It does not require you to purchase a home.
- It does not dictate a standard commission.
- Agent compensation is **fully negotiable**.
- It does not guarantee that a seller will pay your agent’s compensation.
- It does not replace your lender’s loan approval or your attorney’s legal advice.

### How Buyer-Agent Compensation May Be Addressed

Depending on the agreement and transaction, compensation may come from:

- A seller or listing broker concession or payment
- A buyer payment
- A negotiated combination of sources

Any seller contribution must be requested or negotiated where appropriate and documented in the contract or other required forms. Your obligation depends on the written agreement you sign.

> **Important:** Compensation cannot be open-ended and should be stated objectively—for example, as a specific amount or percentage. Your REALTOR® will review the terms and answer your questions before you sign.

---

# SIDE 2 — FROM SEARCH TO CLOSING

**Suggested Word layout:** Landscape • Three columns • 0.5-inch margins  
**Suggested visuals:** Small line icons for search, document review, offer, inspection, financing, and keys

---

## PANEL 4 — HOME SEARCH & PRE-OFFER DETAILS

### 2. The Home Search Process

Your REALTOR® helps turn hundreds of possibilities into a focused search by:

- Creating a customized property search
- Monitoring new listings, price changes, and status updates
- Identifying properties that match your criteria
- Researching available property and community information
- Coordinating showing appointments and routes
- Communicating with listing agents before and after tours
- Helping you compare homes objectively
- Tracking favorites and refining the search
- Identifying potential resale or marketability considerations
- Providing information on neighborhoods and nearby resources without steering
- Recommending appropriate specialists when needed

### Gated-Community Review

For a gated Sarasota-area community, we may investigate:

- HOA or community fees and what they cover
- Amenity access, hours, and additional charges
- Membership requirements
- Buyer application or approval procedures
- Pet, parking, rental, and vehicle restrictions
- Architectural and exterior-maintenance rules
- Transfer, capital-contribution, or initiation fees
- Pending or recent special assessments
- Available budgets, reserves, meeting minutes, and governing documents
- Gate access, guest procedures, and community-maintenance responsibilities

### 3. Pre-Offer Details

Before recommending an offer strategy, your REALTOR® may:

- Confirm the property’s current status and offer instructions
- Review comparable sales and relevant active competition
- Discuss pricing, demand, and days on market
- Ask about known deadlines or competing offers
- Review available seller disclosures and property information
- Identify personal-property inclusions or exclusions
- Discuss financing, appraisal, inspection, and closing-date considerations
- Estimate transaction costs and funds needed at closing
- Identify HOA, permit, insurance, flood, or title questions requiring investigation
- Help you assess the home’s strengths, concerns, and potential negotiating points

> Your REALTOR® provides market guidance—not legal, tax, engineering, insurance, lending, or inspection advice. Qualified specialists should evaluate matters outside the scope of a real estate license.

---

## PANEL 5 — OFFER & NEGOTIATION

### 4. The Offer Process

Once you select a home, your REALTOR® helps you prepare a thoughtful, complete offer.

Services commonly include:

- Explaining available Florida contract forms and major provisions
- Preparing the offer according to your instructions
- Helping you select an offer price and earnest-money deposit
- Discussing financing and appraisal provisions
- Discussing inspection periods and other potential contingencies
- Addressing closing date, occupancy, and possession
- Identifying requested seller concessions or credits
- Including applicable personal-property terms and addenda
- Confirming signatures, initials, dates, and required documents
- Submitting the offer and proof of funds or preapproval as appropriate
- Confirming receipt with the listing side
- Presenting the merits of your offer
- Communicating updates and responding to questions
- Reviewing counteroffers
- Helping you compare price and non-price terms
- Negotiating under your direction
- Delivering the final agreement and supporting documents to appropriate parties

### A Strong Offer Is More Than Price

Your strategy may also consider:

- Deposit amount
- Financing strength
- Appraisal terms
- Inspection period
- Requested repairs or credits
- Seller-paid buyer costs
- Closing timeline
- Post-closing occupancy
- Included furnishings or fixtures
- HOA approval timing
- Seller priorities and market competition

### Before You Sign

Make sure you understand:

1. What you are offering  
2. Which deadlines apply  
3. Which deposits are due and when  
4. What protections or contingencies are included  
5. What could place your deposit at risk  
6. Which costs you may owe at closing  
7. When the offer expires  

---

## PANEL 6 — CONTRACT TO CLOSING

### 5. Contract to Closing

An accepted contract begins a deadline-driven process. Your REALTOR® helps keep the transaction organized by:

- Distributing the executed contract to relevant parties
- Tracking contractual dates and obligations
- Coordinating delivery of escrow deposits
- Communicating with the lender, title company, listing agent, and other professionals
- Helping schedule inspections
- Facilitating access for inspectors, appraisers, and contractors
- Reviewing available inspection findings with you
- Preparing or communicating repair requests as directed
- Monitoring the financing and appraisal process
- Following up on required lender documentation and milestones
- Assisting with HOA or community application procedures
- Monitoring title, survey, permit, disclosure, and association-document issues
- Discussing available options when a concern arises
- Coordinating the final walk-through
- Confirming utilities, identification, wire instructions, and closing logistics
- Reviewing the settlement statement for apparent discrepancies
- Confirming completion of agreed-upon items when possible
- Attending or supporting closing
- Coordinating keys, remotes, access devices, and possession
- Remaining available after closing for real estate-related questions

### Your Contract-to-Close Checklist

- [ ] Deliver escrow deposit by the deadline  
- [ ] Submit all lender documents promptly  
- [ ] Schedule inspections  
- [ ] Obtain insurance and flood quotes early  
- [ ] Review HOA documents and complete any application  
- [ ] Respond quickly to e-signature and information requests  
- [ ] Avoid new credit, large purchases, or job changes without lender guidance  
- [ ] Verify wiring instructions by calling a trusted, independently verified number  
- [ ] Conduct the final walk-through  
- [ ] Bring approved identification and required funds to closing  

### Welcome Home

Your REALTOR® is your central point of coordination—not just the person who opens the door. From consultation and property research to negotiation, inspections, financing coordination, and closing, professional buyer representation helps you make informed decisions at every milestone.

## READY TO BEGIN?

**Schedule your buyer consultation today.**

**[Agent Name], REALTOR®**  
**[Brokerage Name]**  
[Phone] • [Email] • [Website]

---

# FOOTER FOR BOTH SIDES

**Educational notice:** This brochure provides general information and is not legal, tax, lending, insurance, inspection, engineering, title, or association-management advice. Contract terms, brokerage relationships, compensation arrangements, and property-specific requirements vary. Buyers should review all agreements carefully and consult appropriate licensed professionals.

**Fair Housing:** Equal Housing Opportunity. Property searches and recommendations will be conducted in compliance with federal, state, and local fair-housing laws. Buyers choose the communities and properties they wish to consider.

**Source acknowledgment:** Service examples were selected and organized from the topics represented in *132 Things REALTORS® Do for Buyers*, supplemented with Florida transaction and gated-community considerations. REALTOR® is a registered trademark identifying members of the National Association of REALTORS®.

---

# WORD FORMATTING GUIDE

| Element | Recommended treatment |
|---|---|
| Page setup | Letter size, landscape, two pages, double-sided printing, flip on short edge |
| Layout | Three equal columns on each page |
| Headings | Aptos Display or Montserrat, 18–24 pt |
| Body | Aptos, Calibri, or Source Sans, 9.5–10.5 pt |
| Colors | Navy `#173B57`, teal `#2C7C82`, sea-glass `#DDEEEE`, sand `#E9D7B5` |
| Front image | Full-width gated-community or Sarasota-home image across upper third |
| Icons | Consultation, search, checklist, offer, contract, key |
| Callout boxes | Light sea-glass fill with navy headings |
| Printing | Use high-resolution, properly licensed images; test fold and margins before printing |

### Recommended Panel Order for a Tri-Fold

If the brochure will be folded rather than simply printed as a two-sided handout:

- **Outside page, left to right:** Back panel • Fold-in flap • Front cover  
- **Inside page, left to right:** Consultation/Search • Pre-Offer/Offer • Contract-to-Closing  

Before distribution, replace all bracketed placeholders and add brokerage-required disclosures, logo, license information, and Equal Housing Opportunity logo.

- **Target aircraft arrival:** approximately 8:00 AM  
- **Wheels up:** 9:00 AM  

Retain the 8:00 AM departure only if the aviation handler confirms, in writing, that:

1. the aircraft is fully fueled, catered and permit-ready;
2. passports and manifest have been advance-processed where lawful;
3. the SUV has approved airside access;
4. the transfer route and timing are operationally viable; and
5. no additional customs, immigration or security processing is expected.

# Workbook-Level Concierge Notes

## Required Confirmations Before Final Issue

| Priority | Item | Action |
|---|---|---|
| Critical | Calendar year | Add the year and correct weekdays to every tab and booking. |
| Critical | Istanbul airport | Replace “ISL” with the handler-confirmed airport identifier—most likely IST/LTFM. |
| Critical | Aircraft feasibility | Confirm aircraft model, range, technical stops, permits and customs routing in both directions. |
| Critical | June 4 departure | Validate or advance the 8:00 AM hotel pickup. |
| High | Hotel early access | Guarantee occupied/blocked rooms from the prior night for direct access at 4:30 AM June 2. |
| High | Oguz | Obtain full name, license, mobile number, photo and confirmation; otherwise deploy the comparable licensed guide. |
| High | General Manager | Request current GM biography and direct confirmation from the hotel executive office. |
| High | Hidden Garden | Confirm exact restaurant, street address and reservation. |
| High | Maserto / Bespoke Tuxedo | Reconcile vendor names and confirm whether both entries refer to the same garment. |
| High | Samira Lowell | Obtain official portfolio, direct contact, credentials and team roster; otherwise appoint a vetted luxury hotel-recommended artist. |
| High | Adile Sultan Palace | Confirm invitation time, vehicle entrance, staging permission and wedding security contact. |
| Standard | Dining | Reconfirm reservations under Smith, dietary restrictions, preferred tables and cancellation terms. |
| Standard | Ground transport | Add driver names, mobile numbers, vehicle models/colors and license plates 24 hours before each movement. |

## Discreet High-Value Networking Opportunities

These are optional and should only be pursued through warm introductions, with no disruption to the wedding program.

| Contact / Institution | Relevance | Suggested Approach | Link |
|---|---|---|---|
| Four Seasons Bosphorus General Manager | Hospitality leadership, Istanbul network and local introductions | Use the scheduled June 2 meeting; request the current biography directly from the executive office. | [Four Seasons Bosphorus](https://www.fourseasons.com/bosphorus/) |
| Ali Sabancı / Esas Holding | Turkish entrepreneurship, private equity and venture ecosystem | Seek a warm introduction through mutual investors or family-office networks; do not cold-contact during this short trip. | [Esas Holding](https://www.esas.com.tr/en/) |
| Bülent Eczacıbaşı / Eczacıbaşı Holding | Industry, culture, philanthropy and Turkish business leadership | Consider a future private museum or foundation engagement rather than compressing into this itinerary. | [Eczacıbaşı Holding](https://www.eczacibasi.com.tr/en) |
| İKSV leadership | Arts, culture and Istanbul institutional network | Suitable for a future cultural salon, festival or foundation-level introduction. | [Istanbul Foundation for Culture and Arts](https://www.iksv.org/en) |
| Endeavor Türkiye network | High-growth founders and investors | Ask the principal’s existing venture network for a curated founder introduction. | [Endeavor Türkiye](https://www.endeavor.org.tr/) |

## Service Standards

- All drivers stage **30 minutes early** and remain dedicated during each engagement.
- No vendor receives room-floor access without prior ID verification and hotel security clearance.
- Every reservation is reconfirmed at **72 hours and 24 hours**.
- Concierge maintains a live luggage manifest, movement log and single secure contact sheet.
- Principal-facing itinerary should show only necessary contacts; operational vendor details belong in a restricted staff version.
- Security receives primary/alternate routes, venue access requirements, emergency medical locations and a communications plan.
- All medical, dietary, passport and personal data must be stored and transmitted securely.

# Standard Operating Guide  
## Opening a New Rental Agreement at an Airport Location

**Document type:** New Clerk Training Guide  
**Applies to:** Counter and customer-service rental clerks  
**System scope:** Generic reservation, rental, payment, and fleet-management systems  
**Purpose:** Enable clerks to open accurate, compliant Rental Agreements independently, including during peak periods

---

## 1. Purpose and Core Principles

A Rental Agreement is the binding record of the transaction between the rental company and the renter. It must accurately identify:

- The customer and any authorized drivers
- The assigned vehicle
- The rental period and return location
- Rates, taxes, fees, optional products, and estimated total
- Payment and authorization information
- Coverage choices and customer acknowledgments
- Fuel, mileage, and vehicle-condition terms

A well-prepared agreement protects the customer, the company, and the fleet. It also reduces billing disputes, vehicle-control problems, and delays at return.

### Follow these principles for every rental

1. **Verify—do not assume.**
2. **Use original, valid documents whenever required.**
3. **Match the person, reservation, documents, and payment method.**
4. **Explain material charges and terms before obtaining acceptance.**
5. **Never bypass system controls or company policy to save time.**
6. **Protect customer and payment information.**
7. **Escalate unusual cases rather than improvising.**

> **Important:** Company policy, local law, airport rules, card-network requirements, and contractual programs take priority over this guide. Ask a supervisor about exceptions or uncertain eligibility.

---

## 2. Before the Shift: Prepare the Workstation

Complete these checks before serving customers, especially before expected flight-arrival periods.

### Preparation checklist

- Sign in using your own credentials.
- Confirm access to the reservation, fleet, rental, and payment functions.
- Check card terminal, printer, scanner, and document supply.
- Review available vehicle inventory and out-of-service units.
- Review expected arrivals, delayed flights, and high-demand classes.
- Check current wait-time or upgrade procedures.
- Confirm after-hours return and roadside-assistance information.
- Know which manager is handling approvals and escalations.
- Keep keys and printed customer information secured.

### Why this is necessary

Preparation prevents avoidable interruptions at the counter and helps preserve limited vehicle inventory.

### Efficiency tips

- Keep only approved quick-reference material at the workstation.
- Review special reservations before the rush, such as long rentals, one-way rentals, premium vehicles, or unusual arrival times.
- Resolve equipment problems before opening another transaction.

### Common mistakes and troubleshooting

| Problem | Correct action |
|---|---|
| Printer or card terminal is not working | Stop before taking payment or promising a vehicle. Follow technical-support procedures or move to an approved workstation. |
| Inventory shown in the system appears inaccurate | Reconcile with the fleet team. Do not assign a vehicle that is not confirmed ready. |
| Another employee is signed in | Sign them out according to policy and use your own credentials. Never share accounts. |

---

# 3. Step-by-Step Rental Agreement Procedure

## Step 1: Welcome the Customer and Establish the Rental Request

### Actions

1. Greet the customer promptly and professionally.
2. Ask whether the customer has a reservation.
3. Confirm the customer’s name and general request.
4. If appropriate, acknowledge the wait and explain that you will verify the reservation and documents.
5. Observe accessibility, language, or communication needs and provide approved assistance.

**Suggested opening:**

> “Welcome. May I have the name on the reservation and your driver’s license, please?”

### Why this is necessary

A clear opening establishes the purpose of the visit, begins identity verification, and reassures the customer that the transaction is moving forward.

### Efficiency tips

- Request the reservation name and license at the beginning.
- Ask one clear question at a time.
- Keep the conversation focused without appearing rushed.

### Common mistakes and troubleshooting

- **Mistake:** Starting an agreement before confirming whether a reservation exists.  
  **Correction:** Search thoroughly first to avoid duplicate bookings or incorrect rates.

- **Mistake:** Discussing another customer’s details aloud.  
  **Correction:** Use discreet verification questions and protect the screen from public view.

- **Problem:** Language barrier.  
  **Action:** Use approved translation resources; do not guess at consent or rely on an unapproved bystander for sensitive explanations.

---

## Step 2: Locate and Verify the Reservation

### Actions

1. Search using the reservation number when available.
2. If necessary, search by:
   - Renter’s last name
   - First and last name
   - Arrival date and time
   - Loyalty or customer number
   - Flight number, if recorded
3. Confirm the following with the customer:
   - Full renter name
   - Pickup date, time, and location
   - Expected return date, time, and location
   - Reserved vehicle class
   - Quoted rate or program
   - Flight information, if relevant
   - Included or prepaid items
   - Special requests
4. Check reservation notes, alerts, eligibility conditions, and rate restrictions.
5. Confirm whether the reservation is active, prepaid, guaranteed, canceled, duplicated, or marked as a no-show.

### Why this is necessary

Selecting the wrong reservation can cause incorrect pricing, duplicate charges, inventory errors, or unauthorized access to another customer’s information.

### Efficiency tips

- Verify at least two identifying details before opening the record.
- Read notes before promising a vehicle or rate.
- Keep the original reservation number attached to the agreement when required.
- Confirm return location early because one-way rentals may have restrictions or added fees.

### Common mistakes and troubleshooting

| Situation | Response |
|---|---|
| Reservation cannot be found | Check spelling, alternate names, date, booking channel, and confirmation number. Confirm the customer is at the correct rental brand and airport terminal. |
| Multiple similar reservations appear | Compare confirmation numbers, dates, locations, vehicle classes, and booking sources. Do not select based only on the name. |
| Reservation is for another location | Explain the discrepancy and check whether an approved transfer or new booking is possible. Do not silently alter the location or rate. |
| Reservation is prepaid | Verify the prepaid record, named renter, and remaining counter charges. Do not charge the full rental again without confirming what was prepaid. |
| Customer arrived early or late | Confirm whether the reserved rate, vehicle class, and availability still apply. Obtain approval for exceptions when required. |
| Customer wants different dates | Recalculate and disclose any rate, tax, fee, or availability changes before continuing. |

---

## Step 3: Confirm the Rental Itinerary and Customer Needs

### Actions

Ask concise questions to confirm:

- Expected return date and time
- Return location
- Approximate destination or travel area, if relevant to restrictions
- Number of passengers and luggage needs
- Need for additional drivers
- Need for child seats, mobility accommodations, toll products, navigation, or other equipment
- Whether the customer plans to cross a state, provincial, regional, or national border
- Whether the customer expects to take the vehicle on a ferry or into a restricted area
- Preferred fuel or charging return arrangement, when options are offered

### Why this is necessary

The answers can affect vehicle suitability, inventory, pricing, geographic eligibility, equipment availability, and contract terms.

### Efficiency tips

Use one short question:

> “Before I assign the vehicle, has anything changed regarding your return date, return location, number of drivers, or travel plans?”

### Common mistakes and troubleshooting

- **Mistake:** Waiting until the end to discover the customer needs a larger vehicle.  
  **Correction:** Confirm passengers and luggage before assignment.

- **Mistake:** Assuming cross-border travel is allowed.  
  **Correction:** Check policy and documentation requirements before authorizing it.

- **Mistake:** Treating the reservation return time as confirmed without asking.  
  **Correction:** Verify it directly because extensions may affect availability and charges.

---

## Step 4: Obtain and Validate the Driver’s License and Identification

### Actions

1. Request the renter’s physical driver’s license and any additional identification required by policy.
2. Confirm that the license:
   - Is valid and unexpired
   - Belongs to the customer present
   - Displays a recognizable photograph
   - Is valid for the vehicle category
   - Meets minimum licensing-period requirements
   - Is acceptable in the rental jurisdiction
   - Is readable and shows no obvious signs of alteration
3. Compare the customer’s appearance with the photograph.
4. Verify the customer’s date of birth against minimum and maximum age rules.
5. For an international renter, determine whether additional documentation is required, such as:
   - Passport
   - International Driving Permit
   - Translation
   - Entry or travel document
6. Enter information exactly as it appears on the accepted documents:
   - Legal name
   - Date of birth
   - License number
   - Issuing authority
   - Expiration date
   - Address, if required
7. Return documents promptly after use unless an approved procedure requires temporary retention.

### Why this is necessary

License and identity checks establish legal eligibility to drive, support fraud prevention, and ensure that the correct person accepts responsibility for the vehicle.

### Efficiency tips

- Read the document directly rather than asking the customer to recite every field.
- Confirm expiration dates carefully; do not confuse the birth date, issue date, and expiration date.
- Enter names consistently across the reservation, agreement, and payment record.
- Follow approved document-authentication prompts without making accusations.

### Common mistakes and troubleshooting

| Issue | Required response |
|---|---|
| License is expired, suspended, damaged, or unreadable | Do not proceed as though it is valid. Apply company policy and escalate if necessary. |
| Name differs from the reservation | Verify whether there is a legitimate name variation. Do not replace the primary renter without following policy. |
| Name differs from the payment card | Ask about the discrepancy and apply payment-policy rules; do not assume it is acceptable. |
| Customer has only a photograph or copy of a license | Follow policy on digital or copied credentials. Do not accept an image unless specifically permitted. |
| International document is unfamiliar | Use approved verification resources or request supervisor review. |
| Customer does not meet age requirements | Explain applicable restrictions, surcharges, or ineligibility. Do not change the date of birth to force acceptance. |
| Document appears altered | Pause the transaction, protect customer privacy, and follow fraud-escalation procedures. Do not confront the customer or confiscate documents unless authorized. |

---

## Step 5: Record and Confirm Contact Information

### Actions

Obtain and verify:

- Mobile telephone number
- Email address
- Current residential address, when required
- Temporary or local address, when required
- Emergency contact, when policy requires one
- Flight number or travel details, when useful for airport service

Read back or display key contact information for confirmation.

### Why this is necessary

Accurate contact information allows the company to provide the agreement and receipt, communicate about extensions or overdue vehicles, send roadside information, and resolve billing questions.

### Efficiency tips

- Ask the customer to spell the email address slowly.
- Repeat the phone number in grouped digits.
- Confirm which email should receive the Rental Agreement.
- Avoid unnecessary collection of personal information.

### Common mistakes and troubleshooting

- **Mistake:** Copying outdated information from a customer profile without confirmation.  
  **Correction:** Ask whether the phone number, email, and address are current.

- **Mistake:** Entering a mistyped email address.  
  **Correction:** Read it back before finalizing.

- **Problem:** Customer declines required contact information.  
  **Action:** Explain why it is needed and apply policy. Escalate if the agreement cannot legally or operationally proceed.

---

## Step 6: Add and Validate Additional Drivers

### Actions

1. Ask whether anyone else will drive the vehicle.
2. Require each additional driver to be present when company policy requires it.
3. Inspect and validate each additional driver’s license and identification.
4. Confirm age and other eligibility requirements.
5. Add each authorized driver to the agreement.
6. Disclose any additional-driver charge and recognized exemptions.
7. Explain that an unlisted person may not be authorized to drive and may affect contractual protections.

### Why this is necessary

Only properly authorized and eligible drivers should operate the vehicle. Omitting a driver can create legal, coverage, and liability problems.

### Efficiency tips

Ask early:

> “Will anyone other than you drive the vehicle?”

Process all drivers together rather than reopening the agreement later.

### Common mistakes and troubleshooting

- **Mistake:** Treating a spouse, colleague, or family member as automatically authorized.  
  **Correction:** Apply the applicable contract and location policy; exemptions vary.

- **Mistake:** Adding a driver who is not present when presence is required.  
  **Correction:** Explain how the driver may be added later.

- **Problem:** Additional driver lacks acceptable documents.  
  **Action:** Do not list the person as authorized until all requirements are met.

---

## Step 7: Establish the Rate, Rental Period, and Charges

### Actions

1. Confirm the agreed pickup and return details.
2. Verify the rate source and rate code or program, where applicable.
3. Review the pricing structure:
   - Base time-and-mileage rate
   - Estimated rental period
   - Included or limited mileage
   - Taxes
   - Airport concession or facility charges
   - One-way charge
   - Young-driver or other applicable surcharge
   - Additional-driver charge
   - Optional products and equipment
   - Toll or road-use terms
   - Fuel or charging options
   - Deposit or authorization amount
4. Check eligibility for corporate, government, association, loyalty, promotional, or other special rates.
5. Verify required credentials for restricted rates.
6. Explain any difference between the reservation estimate and current estimate before continuing.
7. Obtain approval for manual rate adjustments.

### Why this is necessary

The customer must understand the financial terms, and the agreement must match the valid reservation and eligibility rules.

### Efficiency tips

- Focus on material terms, not only the daily price.
- Separate the **estimated rental charge** from the **payment authorization or deposit**.
- Explain that extensions, late returns, location changes, fuel, tolls, damage, and other post-rental items may change the final total.
- Document approved adjustments immediately.

### Common mistakes and troubleshooting

| Error or question | Correct handling |
|---|---|
| Quoted total does not match | Compare dates, times, tax jurisdiction, vehicle class, optional products, return location, and rate eligibility. |
| Customer presents a discount at pickup | Check whether it is valid for the reservation and whether repricing changes other terms. |
| Restricted rate lacks required proof | Request valid credentials or offer an eligible rate. Do not force the restricted rate. |
| Manual discount is requested | Obtain the required approval and document the reason. |
| Customer focuses only on the daily rate | Explain the estimated total and major taxes and fees before acceptance. |

---

## Step 8: Discuss Coverage and Optional Products Neutrally

### Actions

1. Identify optional coverage or protection products available at the location.
2. Explain each product using approved descriptions, including:
   - What it generally addresses
   - Major exclusions or limitations
   - Price and charging basis
   - Whether it is optional, unless law or contract states otherwise
3. Ask the customer to accept or decline each product as required.
4. Record the selection accurately.
5. Explain that the clerk cannot interpret the customer’s personal insurance policy or credit-card benefits.
6. Present other optional products—such as roadside plans, toll services, child seats, navigation, satellite radio, or fuel plans—with price and key terms.

### Why this is necessary

Optional products can materially affect the customer’s cost and financial responsibility. Clear, neutral disclosure supports informed consent and reduces disputes.

### Efficiency tips

Use a consistent explanation for every customer. For example:

> “I’ll briefly review the available protection and service options, including the price and key terms. You can accept or decline each one.”

### Common mistakes and troubleshooting

- **Mistake:** Saying a protection product provides “full coverage.”  
  **Correction:** Use approved terminology and state relevant exclusions.

- **Mistake:** Telling the customer that personal insurance or a credit card definitely covers the rental.  
  **Correction:** Advise the customer to consult the insurer or card issuer.

- **Mistake:** Adding a product without clear customer acceptance.  
  **Correction:** Remove it and obtain a corrected agreement before vehicle release.

- **Problem:** Customer is unsure.  
  **Action:** Re-explain the product neutrally and allow the customer to decide. Do not pressure or make legal recommendations.

---

## Step 9: Obtain and Validate the Payment Method

### Actions

1. Request an accepted payment method in the renter’s name, unless policy permits otherwise.
2. Confirm:
   - Cardholder name
   - Expiration date
   - Card type
   - Payment-method eligibility
   - Available authorization according to terminal response
3. Process the payment method through the approved terminal.
4. Explain:
   - Estimated rental total
   - Authorization or deposit amount
   - That an authorization is not necessarily the final charge
   - That the issuing bank controls when unused funds become available
5. Complete any additional requirements for debit cards, cash qualification, prepaid cards, digital wallets, or other payment types.
6. Never record prohibited card data or ask for a personal identification number outside the approved terminal.

### Why this is necessary

The payment method secures expected charges and helps establish renter eligibility. Correct handling also protects payment-card data.

### Efficiency tips

- State the authorization amount before processing it.
- Handle the card only as long as necessary.
- Let the customer enter a PIN privately.
- If declined, verify whether the customer has another accepted payment method before restarting the transaction.

### Common mistakes and troubleshooting

| Situation | Correct response |
|---|---|
| Authorization is declined | Retry only if an obvious entry or terminal error occurred. Otherwise, request another accepted method or ask the customer to contact the issuer. |
| Cardholder is not present | Apply third-party payment policy. Do not type card details from a message or photograph unless explicitly authorized by procedure. |
| Card name does not match renter | Verify the reason and apply company policy; escalate exceptions. |
| Debit card has additional conditions | Explain and complete all required checks before assigning the vehicle. |
| Customer believes the authorization is a charge | Explain the difference and that release timing is controlled by the financial institution. |
| Customer wants to split payment | Follow system and policy limitations; do not promise a payment arrangement that cannot be supported. |
| Terminal times out or loses connection | Verify whether an authorization was created before running the card again to avoid duplicate holds. |

> **Data-security rule:** Do not write down, photograph, email, or place full card numbers or security codes in notes.

---

## Step 10: Select and Assign a Suitable Vehicle

### Actions

1. Review available vehicles in the reserved class.
2. Confirm that the selected vehicle is:
   - Available in the fleet system
   - Clean and ready
   - Safe and not marked out of service
   - Appropriate for the customer’s needs
   - Permitted for the planned destination and use
3. Confirm key vehicle data:
   - Unit number
   - License plate
   - Vehicle identification, if required
   - Make, model, color, and class
   - Current mileage
   - Fuel or battery level
   - Parking location
4. Assign the unit to the Rental Agreement.
5. If the reserved class is unavailable, follow the approved substitution or upgrade process.
6. Confirm any upgrade charge before finalizing.

### Why this is necessary

Accurate assignment maintains fleet control and ensures that the agreement describes the vehicle the customer actually receives.

### Efficiency tips

- Assign only a confirmed ready vehicle.
- Give clear directions to the vehicle or shuttle area.
- Consider passenger count, luggage, accessibility, weather, and destination.
- Avoid assigning the final vehicle in a class to a walk-up customer if a confirmed reservation still requires it, unless directed by inventory control.

### Common mistakes and troubleshooting

| Issue | Resolution |
|---|---|
| Reserved class is unavailable | Apologize, check nearby inventory or approved substitutions, explain any difference, and obtain approval where required. |
| Vehicle becomes unavailable after assignment | Unassign it correctly, select another ready unit, and ensure all agreement fields update. |
| Customer requests a lower class | Confirm new rate, capacity, and luggage needs before changing the agreement. |
| Customer requests an upgrade | Disclose whether it is complimentary or charged and state the added amount. |
| Assigned vehicle cannot be found | Contact fleet staff and reassign the agreement; do not send the customer to search indefinitely. |
| Vehicle is dirty, damaged, low on fuel, or unsafe | Replace it or have it corrected before release. Never release an unsafe or out-of-service vehicle. |

---

## Step 11: Verify Vehicle Condition, Fuel or Charge, and Mileage

### Actions

1. Confirm the recorded starting mileage.
2. Confirm the recorded fuel level or battery state of charge.
3. Review the documented condition report.
4. Explain how the customer can report pre-existing damage or a discrepancy.
5. If inspection is available, encourage the customer to inspect the vehicle before departure.
6. Update the record if a legitimate discrepancy is found.
7. Retain inspection evidence according to company procedure.

### Why this is necessary

Accurate starting condition, mileage, and fuel or battery information reduce later disputes and support fair billing.

### Efficiency tips

- Point out where condition and fuel information appears on the agreement.
- Explain the fastest approved method for reporting a discrepancy.
- Record issues before the vehicle leaves whenever possible.

### Common mistakes and troubleshooting

- **Mistake:** Telling the customer that “all damage is already noted” without checking.  
  **Correction:** Direct the customer to inspect and report discrepancies.

- **Problem:** Fuel gauge or battery level differs from the agreement.  
  **Action:** Verify and correct the record or assign another vehicle.

- **Problem:** Customer finds damage after leaving the immediate pickup area.  
  **Action:** Follow the time-stamped reporting procedure and document the notification without promising an outcome beyond your authority.

---

## Step 12: Review the Rental Terms and Customer Responsibilities

### Actions

Review the major terms in plain language:

- Renter and authorized drivers
- Assigned vehicle
- Pickup and expected return date and time
- Return location
- Estimated total and authorization amount
- Rate period and late-return consequences
- Mileage terms
- Fuel or charging return requirement
- Toll handling
- Optional products accepted or declined
- Geographic, road-use, towing, smoking, pet, or other restrictions
- Extension procedure
- Accident, damage, theft, breakdown, and roadside procedures
- Prohibition on unauthorized drivers
- After-hours return process and when responsibility for the vehicle ends
- Possible charges not included in the initial estimate
- Contact information for assistance

Ask whether the customer has questions before obtaining acceptance.

### Why this is necessary

The customer must understand the material obligations before accepting the agreement. A signature alone is not a substitute for clear disclosure.

### Efficiency tips

Use a consistent final summary:

> “You are renting the assigned vehicle through [date and time], returning it to [location]. Your current estimated total is [amount], and the authorization is [amount]. Please return it with [fuel or charge requirement]. Only listed drivers may operate it. Contact us before the return time if you need an extension.”

### Common mistakes and troubleshooting

- **Mistake:** Rushing directly to the signature screen.  
  **Correction:** Summarize the major financial and operational terms first.

- **Mistake:** Stating that the estimate is guaranteed regardless of changes.  
  **Correction:** Explain which events may change the final bill.

- **Problem:** Customer disputes a term.  
  **Action:** Pause, review the reservation and selections, correct errors, and produce an updated agreement before acceptance.

---

## Step 13: Obtain Customer Acceptance and Signature

### Actions

1. Give the customer an opportunity to review the agreement.
2. Direct attention to:
   - Rental dates and locations
   - Vehicle
   - Rate and estimated charges
   - Optional-product choices
   - Fuel or charging terms
   - Authorization
3. Obtain required initials, electronic acknowledgments, and signature.
4. Confirm the signature was captured successfully.
5. Do not sign for the customer or select acceptance on the customer’s behalf.
6. Correct errors and generate a replacement agreement if necessary.

### Why this is necessary

The signature documents the customer’s acceptance of the agreement and selected terms.

### Efficiency tips

- Explain what the customer is acknowledging rather than saying only, “Sign here.”
- Review the completed agreement immediately so errors are corrected before vehicle release.
- Ensure the customer receives the final version, not a draft.

### Common mistakes and troubleshooting

| Issue | Response |
|---|---|
| Customer signs before noticing an error | Correct the agreement and obtain acceptance of the corrected version. |
| Signature device fails | Use the approved alternative procedure; do not imitate or manually enter the customer’s signature. |
| Customer refuses to sign | Identify the concern and correct factual errors. If the required terms remain unacceptable, do not release the vehicle. |
| Customer accidentally accepts an unwanted product | Remove it and reissue the agreement before departure. |

---

## Step 14: Finalize and Issue the Rental Agreement

### Actions

1. Perform a final comparison of:
   - Renter name and license
   - Additional drivers
   - Payment status
   - Rental dates and return location
   - Rate and optional products
   - Assigned vehicle
   - Mileage and fuel or battery level
   - Required signatures and acknowledgments
2. Open the agreement in the rental system.
3. Provide the customer with a paper or electronic copy.
4. Confirm the customer can access the copy.
5. Provide:
   - Vehicle keys or approved pickup instructions
   - Parking location
   - Exit procedure
   - Roadside and emergency contact information
   - Return directions and after-hours instructions
6. Thank the customer and close the interaction professionally.

### Why this is necessary

Finalization activates the contract and transfers the vehicle into rental status. A final check prevents a customer from leaving with an incomplete or inaccurate agreement.

### Efficiency tips

Use a brief “name–car–date–place–price–payment–signature” check before releasing keys:

1. Correct **name**
2. Correct **car**
3. Correct return **date**
4. Correct return **place**
5. Correct **price**
6. Approved **payment**
7. Captured **signature**

### Common mistakes and troubleshooting

- **Mistake:** Releasing keys before the agreement is fully open.  
  **Correction:** Never release a vehicle until the system confirms completion.

- **Mistake:** Sending the agreement to an unverified email address.  
  **Correction:** Confirm the address and resend if necessary.

- **Problem:** System fails during finalization.  
  **Action:** Determine whether the agreement opened before attempting it again. Follow downtime procedures and obtain authorization before releasing any vehicle.

---

## Step 15: Complete Post-Transaction Tasks

### Actions

1. Secure or return all documents.
2. Dispose of unwanted printouts in approved confidential-waste containers.
3. Update fleet or key-control records if not completed automatically.
4. Record approved notes that are factual, relevant, and professional.
5. Notify fleet or management of:
   - Inventory discrepancies
   - Damaged or unsafe vehicles
   - Unresolved customer issues
   - Suspected fraud
   - Special return arrangements
6. Clear the screen before serving the next customer.

### Why this is necessary

Proper closure protects customer data, supports fleet accountability, and prevents errors from carrying into the next transaction.

### Efficiency tips

Complete post-transaction tasks immediately. Unfinished notes and key records are easy to forget during a rush.

### Common mistakes and troubleshooting

- **Mistake:** Leaving identity or payment information visible.  
  **Correction:** Return documents, lock the screen, and secure or destroy printouts according to policy.

- **Mistake:** Writing emotional or speculative notes.  
  **Correction:** Record only objective facts and approved actions.

---

# 4. Peak-Hour Workflow

Speed should come from preparation and consistency—not from skipping controls.

## Recommended sequence

1. Greet the customer and request reservation name and license.
2. Locate and verify the reservation.
3. Confirm itinerary and additional drivers.
4. Validate all required documents.
5. Confirm contact details.
6. Verify rate and eligibility.
7. Present optional products.
8. Obtain payment authorization.
9. Assign a ready vehicle.
10. Review material terms.
11. Obtain signature.
12. Finalize, provide the agreement, and release keys.

## Ways to work faster without creating risk

- Ask for documents at the beginning.
- Read reservation notes before discussing changes.
- Use a consistent explanation of rates and optional products.
- Keep the customer informed while the system processes.
- Resolve one exception completely before moving to the next.
- Use a supervisor for exceptions instead of repeatedly attempting unsupported changes.
- Do not begin a second customer’s agreement while the first customer’s documents or payment information are exposed.
- Never skip identity, payment, vehicle-readiness, or signature checks.

---

# 5. Common Exceptions and Troubleshooting

## A. No Reservation or Walk-Up Customer

1. Check available inventory.
2. Ask for dates, return location, vehicle needs, and destination.
3. Quote the estimated total and key restrictions.
4. Create a new reservation or proceed according to walk-up procedures.
5. Complete all normal identity, payment, eligibility, and signature checks.

**Do not promise a vehicle before confirming a ready unit and payment eligibility.**

---

## B. Customer Is at the Wrong Brand, Terminal, or Location

1. Verify the reservation confirmation.
2. Explain the mismatch courteously.
3. Determine whether an approved transfer, shuttle, or new reservation is possible.
4. Clearly disclose any pricing difference.
5. Avoid criticizing another rental company or location.

---

## C. Customer Arrives Before the Vehicle Is Ready

1. Verify the reservation and expected ready time.
2. Check for an equivalent ready unit.
3. Offer approved alternatives.
4. Give an honest estimated wait time.
5. Avoid marking a vehicle ready until cleaning and safety checks are complete.

---

## D. Reserved Vehicle Class Is Sold Out

1. Verify that no ready units are available.
2. Check approved upgrade, substitution, downgrade, or transfer options.
3. Explain passenger and luggage implications.
4. Disclose any price change.
5. Obtain required authorization and document the resolution.

**Never quietly downgrade the customer or add an upgrade charge without consent.**

---

## E. Payment Authorization Is Declined

1. Confirm the amount and terminal response.
2. Check for a clear processing error.
3. Avoid repeated attempts that may create multiple holds.
4. Request another accepted payment method.
5. Allow the customer to contact the issuer privately.
6. Do not state that the customer lacks funds; the clerk does not know the issuer’s reason.

---

## F. Identification or License Is Unacceptable

1. Explain the specific policy requirement neutrally.
2. Ask whether the customer has another acceptable document.
3. Consider whether another eligible person can become the renter under normal policy—not merely be substituted into the original renter’s agreement.
4. Escalate uncertain international or digital credentials.
5. Do not alter data to bypass an eligibility rule.

---

## G. System Is Unavailable

1. Notify a supervisor or technical support.
2. Determine whether company-approved downtime procedures apply.
3. Secure documents and payment data.
4. Do not repeatedly authorize the same card.
5. Do not release a vehicle unless the authorized contingency process permits it.
6. Enter or reconcile the transaction as soon as systems return.

---

## H. Customer Requests a Change After Signing

Before the vehicle leaves:

1. Reopen or void the agreement according to procedure.
2. Make the authorized change.
3. Review the new charges and terms.
4. Obtain a new signature or acknowledgment.
5. Issue the corrected agreement.

After the vehicle leaves:

1. Verify the renter’s identity.
2. Follow extension or amendment procedures.
3. Obtain any additional authorization.
4. Send the amended terms and retain the required acknowledgment.

---

## I. Suspected Fraud or Identity Theft

Possible warning signs include:

- Document information that does not match the customer
- Altered or inconsistent identification
- Repeatedly declined cards
- Third-party payment pressure
- Unusual urgency to bypass controls
- Conflicting answers about travel
- Attempts to prevent document inspection

### Response

1. Remain calm and professional.
2. Do not accuse the customer.
3. Follow verification prompts.
4. Contact a supervisor or security through approved channels.
5. Protect documents and personal information.
6. Do not release the vehicle until the concern is resolved.

---

## J. Customer Becomes Upset

1. Listen without interrupting.
2. Restate the issue.
3. Separate facts from requested outcomes.
4. Explain what you can do.
5. Offer approved alternatives.
6. Escalate threats, discrimination concerns, safety risks, or policy exceptions.
7. Do not argue, retaliate, or make promises outside your authority.

Useful phrase:

> “I understand the concern. Let me verify the reservation and available options so I can give you an accurate solution.”

---

# 6. Errors That Must Never Be Used as Shortcuts

Never:

- Open an agreement under the wrong customer.
- Change a date of birth, license detail, or address to pass eligibility.
- Use another employee’s login or approval credentials.
- Sign or accept terms for a customer.
- Add optional products without consent.
- Release an out-of-service or unconfirmed vehicle.
- Release keys before the agreement is finalized.
- Promise personal insurance or card coverage.
- Write down full payment-card details or security codes.
- Copy documents using a personal phone.
- Ignore a declined authorization.
- Override a rate or fee without authority.
- List an ineligible or absent driver contrary to policy.
- Conceal a price change.
- Leave customer information visible to the next person in line.

---

# 7. Final Counter Checklist

Use this checklist before releasing every vehicle.

## Customer and documents

- [ ] Correct reservation selected
- [ ] Primary renter is present
- [ ] Identity matches the reservation and documents
- [ ] Driver’s license is valid and acceptable
- [ ] Age and licensing requirements are met
- [ ] International documents are complete, if applicable
- [ ] Additional drivers are verified and listed
- [ ] Contact details are current

## Rental details

- [ ] Pickup and return dates and times are correct
- [ ] Return location is correct
- [ ] Rate and eligibility have been verified
- [ ] Taxes, fees, surcharges, and one-way charges are included
- [ ] Optional products are accurately accepted or declined
- [ ] Fuel, charging, toll, and mileage terms are correct
- [ ] Estimated total has been explained

## Payment

- [ ] Payment method is acceptable
- [ ] Cardholder requirements are met
- [ ] Authorization is approved
- [ ] Authorization or deposit amount has been explained
- [ ] No prohibited card information has been recorded

## Vehicle

- [ ] Vehicle is assigned to this agreement
- [ ] Unit is clean, safe, ready, and not out of service
- [ ] Vehicle class is correct or substitution is approved
- [ ] License plate and unit data are accurate
- [ ] Starting mileage is recorded
- [ ] Fuel or battery level is recorded
- [ ] Existing condition is documented
- [ ] Parking location and keys match the assigned vehicle

## Agreement and release

- [ ] Material terms were reviewed
- [ ] Customer had an opportunity to ask questions
- [ ] Required signatures and acknowledgments were captured
- [ ] Agreement is confirmed open in the system
- [ ] Customer received a paper or electronic copy
- [ ] Return and roadside instructions were provided
- [ ] Keys were released only after finalization

---

# 8. Suggested Standard Closing

> “Your vehicle is a [color, make/model or class] in space [location]. The agreement shows a return to [location] by [date and time]. Please return it with [fuel or charging requirement]. Only the drivers listed on the agreement may operate it. If you need an extension or have a problem with the vehicle, contact us before the return time using the number on your agreement. Thank you, and have a safe trip.”

---

# 9. Quick Reference: When to Escalate

Contact a supervisor or authorized specialist when:

- Identity, license, or payment documents appear altered or inconsistent.
- The renter does not meet standard eligibility rules.
- The required payment authorization cannot be obtained.
- A restricted rate lacks proof of eligibility.
- The reserved class is unavailable and no normal substitution exists.
- A customer requests a manual rate override or policy exception.
- The system is down and vehicle release is being considered.
- A vehicle is unsafe, missing, damaged, or incorrectly recorded.
- The customer disputes contract language or alleges unauthorized charges.
- There is a threat, safety issue, suspected fraud, or legal concern.
- You are uncertain whether an action is permitted.

> **Final rule:** When in doubt, pause the transaction, protect the customer’s information, keep the customer informed, and obtain authorized guidance before releasing the vehicle.

# 1. Executive Summary & Property Highlights ![Restaurant storefront — free stock photo](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1555396273-367ea4eb4db5?auto=format&fit=crop&w=1600&q=80) *Suggested free stock source: Unsplash. Search term: “restaurant storefront.”* ## Executive Summary The subject opportunity is a **5,000 SF end cap** within a **32,000 SF neighborhood shopping center** at **123 Dade County Rd, Miami, Florida**, shadow-anchored by **Publix**. The combination of grocery-driven trips, strong end-cap visibility, and demonstrated submarket demand for quick-service restaurants creates a compelling platform for restaurant operators seeking access, branding, and repeat customer traffic. The leasing team’s objective is to identify and convert qualified QSR prospects through a disciplined system: 1. Build a targeted list by category, geography, and expansion profile. 2. Lead with QSR-specific benefits—not generic retail language. 3. Qualify operational and financial requirements early. 4. Maintain a coordinated 21-business-day outreach cadence. 5. Drive prospects to a site visit and written proposal. 6. Track every touchpoint, objection, and next action in the CRM. ## Property Positioning ### Core Pitch > **A highly visible 5,000 SF end cap in a Publix shadow-anchored Miami neighborhood center, offering a QSR operator the opportunity to capture grocery-linked traffic, local meal occasions, delivery demand, and prominent storefront exposure.** ### Confirmed Property Facts | Attribute | Property Information | |---|---| | Address | 123 Dade County Rd, Miami, FL | | Center type | Neighborhood shopping center | | Center size | 32,000 SF | | Available space | 5,000 SF | | Configuration | End cap | | Anchor relationship | Shadow-anchored by Publix | | Market signal | Strong submarket demand for QSR tenants | | Primary use target | Quick-service and fast-casual restaurants | ## QSR-Relevant Highlights - **End-cap visibility:** Stronger branding, signage potential, and customer recognition than typical inline space. - **Publix adjacency:** Potential exposure to frequent grocery trips and convenience-oriented consumers. - **5,000 SF footprint:** Can accommodate a larger-format fast-casual concept, flagship QSR, multi-daypart restaurant, or potentially divisible concepts, subject to ownership and code review. - **Neighborhood-center setting:** Supports repeat local visits, takeout, delivery, and routine meal occasions. - **Miami location:** Access to a diverse consumer base and a restaurant-active marketplace. - **Category demand:** QSR demand supports a focused campaign rather than a broad, undifferentiated retail search. ## Items to Verify Before Prospecting Never represent an unconfirmed item as fact. Obtain and document: - Asking rent, CAM, taxes, insurance, and annual escalations - Delivery condition and landlord work - Existing kitchen infrastructure, if any - Electrical capacity, gas availability, grease-trap capacity, and plumbing - Exhaust routing and rooftop penetration rights - HVAC condition and tonnage - Permitted use and zoning - Drive-thru feasibility, pickup lane, and curbside options - Patio potential - Signage criteria and pylon-panel availability - Parking ratio and loading access - Exclusive-use restrictions and prohibited uses - Delivery timing and ownership’s target economics - Divisibility and minimum acceptable premises size - Traffic counts, demographics, and Publix performance data, if legally available > **Broker standard:** Say “subject to verification” until engineering, zoning, ownership, and lease documents confirm a physical or legal capability.
# 2. Target QSR Tenant Categories ![Fast-casual meal — free stock photo](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1504674900247-0877df9cc836?auto=format&fit=crop&w=1600&q=80) *Suggested free stock source: Unsplash. Search term: “fast casual food.”* ## Prospecting Priorities Prioritize operators with: - Active Florida or Southeast expansion plans - Existing Miami-Dade operations or nearby franchisees - A footprint requirement compatible with 5,000 SF - Strong takeout, delivery, and digital ordering capabilities - Financial capacity to build out and operate the premises - Proven unit economics and multi-unit operating experience - Ability to use the end cap’s visibility and grocery adjacency - Reasonable parking, venting, grease, utility, and access requirements ## Category Matrix | Category | Ideal Prospect Profile | Why the Site May Fit | Key Qualification Questions | |---|---|---|---| | **Fast casual** | Regional or national operators; bowls, Mediterranean, Mexican, Asian, burgers, salads | 5,000 SF may support seating, pickup, catering, and a broad kitchen platform | Target size? Dine-in versus carryout mix? | | **Subs / sandwiches** | National franchise systems, regional sandwich brands, deli concepts | Strong lunch, takeout, catering, and grocery-trip compatibility | Franchisee identified? Catering need? Prototype size? Cold storage requirements? | | **Chicken / wings** | Fried chicken, grilled chicken, tenders, wings, rotisserie concepts | High consumer demand and strong takeout/delivery orientation | Fryer package? Hood length? Grease capacity? Odor mitigation? Pickup traffic? | | **Smoothies / health** | Smoothies, juice, açaí, wellness cafés, protein-focused concepts | Complements grocery and lifestyle visits; often lower venting burden | Is 5,000 SF too large? Divisibility? Co-tenancy? Daypart and seating needs? | ## Recommended Priority Tiers ### Tier 1 — Immediate Focus - Fast-casual operators seeking 3,000–5,000 SF - Chicken/wings concepts with proven Florida operations - Larger coffee/breakfast concepts not dependent on a drive-thru - Pizza concepts combining dine-in, carryout, and delivery - Multi-unit franchisees controlling local development rights ### Tier 2 — Strategic Prospects - Subs and sandwich brands with catering programs - Regional concepts entering Miami-Dade - Health-focused concepts capable of using a larger premises - Operators that may use the site as a flagship or training location ### Tier 3 — Conditional Prospects - Concepts requiring a drive-thru - Prospects requiring major utility or structural modifications - Small-format users unless the space is divisible - Startups without restaurant operating history or adequate capitalization ## Build the Prospect Universe Each agent should source prospects from: - Existing tenant and franchisee relationships - Shopping-center and restaurant databases available to the brokerage - Local drive tours and competitor-center tenant rosters - Restaurant openings, permits, and expansion announcements - Franchise development directories - LinkedIn searches for real estate, development, franchise, and operations executives - Referrals from restaurant architects, contractors, equipment vendors, and attorneys - # 3. Prospecting, Qualification & Pitch Framework ![Restaurant kitchen — free stock photo](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1556910103-1c02745aae4d?auto=format&fit=crop&w=1600&q=80) *Suggested free stock source: Unsplash. Concept category and typical footprint 3. Whether the operator is corporate or franchised 4. Likely decision-maker 5. One credible reason the property may fit 6. One operational issue that requires qualification 7. The specific next step being requested ## QSR Pitch Structure: **V.I.S.I.T.** Use this structure in calls, emails, and tours. ### **V — Visibility** Lead with the 5,000 SF end-cap position and storefront exposure. ### **I — Integrated Trip Demand** Explain the potential benefit of being in a neighborhood center shadow-anchored by Publix. ### **S — Space Fit** Connect the 5,000 SF footprint to the prospect’s prototype, seating, kitchen, pickup, delivery, or catering program. ### **I — Infrastructure Due Diligence** Acknowledge that utilities, venting, grease, access, and permitting will be verified. Do not overpromise. ### **T — Tour and Test** Ask the prospect to review the flyer/site plan and schedule a site visit. ## Discovery Questions ### Real Estate Strategy - Which South Florida trade areas are priorities during the next 12–24 months? - Are you expanding through corporate stores, franchisees, or both? - What is your preferred and acceptable footprint? - Do you have an approved franchisee or operator for Miami-Dade? - What co-tenancy or adjacency matters most? ### Operations - Is a drive-thru required, preferred, or unnecessary? - What are your hood, grease, gas, electrical, and HVAC requirements? - How many seats and pickup positions are needed? - What percentage of sales is dine-in, takeout, delivery, and catering? - Do you need patio space, dedicated delivery parking, or rear loading? - What are your anticipated hours and peak periods? ### Economics and Timing - What rent range does the prototype support? - What landlord contribution or delivery condition is required? - What is the target opening date? - How long are design, permitting, construction, and franchisor approvals? - Who approves the site, lease, and capital expenditure? ### Financial Qualification Request only through approved company procedures: - Operating history and existing-unit performance - Franchise approval or development agreement - Financial statements or proof of funds - Principal/operator résumé - Proposed guaranty structure - Store-opening budget and financing plan ## Qualification Scorecard Score each item from **0 to 2**. | Criterion | 0 | 1 | 2 | |---|---|---|---| | Geographic fit | No Miami plan | Exploratory | Active Miami-Dade requirement | | Prototype fit | Material mismatch | Adaptable | Fits 5,000 SF | | Operational feasibility | Major conflict | Requires study | Likely feasible | | Decision-maker access | Unknown | Influencer | Direct authority | | Operator strength | Unproven | Some experience | Proven multi-unit/corporate | | Financial capacity | Unknown/weak | Under review | Demonstrated | | Timing | Over 24 months | 12–24 months | Within 12 months | | Engagement | Unresponsive | Reviewing | Tour/proposal requested | **Priority classification:** - **13–16:** Hot—senior broker involvement and immediate tour/proposal - **9–12:** Warm—continue discovery and resolve feasibility issues - **5–8:** Nurture—monthly follow-up - **0–4:** Low priority—archive unless circumstances change ## Objection Responses | Objection | Suggested Response | |---|---| | “5,000 SF is too large.” | “Understood. What is your ideal range? I will confirm whether ownership will consider demising the end cap or whether a larger-format prototype, catering component, or complementary use could make the space work.” | | “We require a drive-thru.” | “Is the drive-thru mandatory or simply preferred? I will verify circulation and entitlement feasibility before suggesting that the site can accommodate it.” | | “We already have a nearby unit.” | “What distance or cannibalization threshold do you use? The grocery-linked trip pattern and end-cap exposure may serve a different customer occasion, but we should test that against your sales map.” | | “Rent is too high.” | “What occupancy-cost level does the prototype support? If the location fits operationally, we can frame the economics around term, delivery condition, tenant improvements, free rent, and guaranty rather than rate alone.” | | “We need more data.” | “I can provide the site plan, photos, verified demographics, traffic information, and utility details as available. Which three items determine whether your team advances a site?” | | “Send information.” | “Absolutely. I will send the package today. May I hold ten minutes on Thursday to get your initial reaction and confirm prototype fit?” |

The opportunity may align with [Brand’s] South Florida expansion. May I send the one-page site summary to the correct real estate contact?
# 5. Outreach Cadence & Follow-Up Strategy ![Calendar and planning — free stock photo](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1506784983877-45594efa4cbe?auto=format&fit=crop&w=1600&q=80) *Suggested free stock source: Unsplash. Search term: “calendar planning desk.”* ## 21-Business-Day Prospecting Cadence | Day | Channel | Action | Objective | |---:|---|---|---| | 1 | Email + call | Send personalized email; call within 30 minutes | Create recognition and seek live qualification | | 2 | LinkedIn | Connect with a short site-specific note | Establish a second channel | | 4 | Call | Reference initial email; ask two qualification questions | Confirm expansion geography and footprint | | 6 | Email | Send one useful item: flyer, site plan, photo, or verified data | Add value without repeating the same message | | 8 | Site visit | Visit an existing location if practical; observe prototype and ask for operator contact without disrupting service | Improve personalization and identify decision-maker | | 10 | Call + voicemail | Use a category-specific benefit or address likely objection | Generate response | | 13 | LinkedIn | Engage professionally or send a brief follow-up | Remain visible | | 15 | Email | Invite prospect to a scheduled tour window | Convert interest into action | | 18 | Call | Ask directly whether the site should remain under consideration | Qualify in or out | | 21 | Breakup email | Request referral or permission to move to periodic updates | Close the sequence professionally | ## Breakup Email **Subject:** Close the File? Miami End-Cap Opportunity > Hi [First Name], > > I have tried to reach you regarding the 5,000 SF end cap at 123 Dade County Rd in Miami. I do not want to crowd your inbox. > > Should I: > 1. Keep [Brand] informed as details develop; > 2. Contact another person on your real estate team; or > 3. Close the file because Miami-Dade or this footprint is not currently a fit? > > A one-line reply is appreciated. > > Best, > [Signature] ## Nurture Cadence After Day 21 - **Hot prospects:** Touch every 2–3 business days; every interaction must advance a defined action. - **Warm prospects:** Weekly contact with new information or a resolution to an open issue. - **Long-range prospects:** Monthly update. - **Inactive prospects:** Quarterly market/site update unless asked to stop. - **Not a fit:** Record the reason and next expansion review date. ## Site-Visit Protocol ### Before the Tour - Confirm date, attendee names, and decision roles. - Send a calendar invitation, map, flyer, and site plan. - Ask what the prospect needs to inspect. - Coordinate access and notify ownership/property management. - Bring measuring device, printed plans, utility information, and qualification notes. - Walk the property in advance; remove avoidable presentation issues. ### During the Tour 1. Meet at the most visible approach to demonstrate exposure. 2. Explain the center layout and Publix relationship accurately. 3. Walk storefront, premises, rear service area, parking, and signage locations. 4. Discuss customer circulation, pickup, delivery, and loading. 5. Ask the prospect to describe the prototype in the space. 6. Identify required technical studies without promising feasibility. 7. Confirm the approval process and timing. 8. Secure a next meeting before leaving. ### After the Tour - Send recap within two hours. - Upload notes and photos to the CRM. - Assign every action to a person and due date. - Obtain ownership guidance on business terms before proposing. - Target an LOI or written site proposal within 3–5 business days for a qualified prospect. ## Weekly Team Operating Rhythm | Timing | Team Activity | |---|---| | Monday, 9:00 a.m. | Pipeline review; assign Tier 1 prospects and weekly targets | | Daily, 9:30–11:00 a.m. | Protected outbound call block | | Daily, 3:30–4:00 p.m. | Follow-up emails and CRM updates | | Wednesday | Drive tours, local operator visits, and referral outreach | | Friday | Metrics review, objection coaching, and next-week commitments | ## Minimum Weekly Activity per Agent - 25 new qualified prospects added - 40 outbound calls - 25 personalized emails - 10 LinkedIn touches - 5 live decision-maker conversations - 2 site-tour invitations - 1 completed site tour or virtual review - 100% CRM completion by Friday ## Core Performance Metrics Track activity and conversion—not activity alone. - Contact-to-conversation rate - Conversation-to-qualified-prospect rate - Qualified-prospect-to-tour rate - Tour-to-proposal rate - Proposal-to-LOI rate - LOI-to-lease rate - Average days between stages - Top disqualification reasons - Lead sources producing the strongest prospects
# 6. One-Page Prospective Tenant Flyer Template ![Retail storefront — free stock photo](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1441986300917-64674bd600d8?auto=format&fit=crop&w=1600&q=80) *Suggested free stock source: Unsplash.
